"We absolutely need to close our borders to international surrogacy," Fell said. "Why do we need folks from overseas coming, renting wombs here in the United States?"
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Hochul dodges when pressed over victims of illegal immigrant crime: ‘Will you apologize?’
summary: Bruce Blakeman pressed Kathy Hochul to apologize to families of victims killed by illegal immigrants, but the governor pivoted to ICE-related deaths.
story: Hochul criticized Immigration and Customs Enforcement after Blakeman asked her to apologize to families of people killed by illegal immigrants during the Oct. 13 debate.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declined to directly apologize to the families of people killed by illegal immigrants after Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman confronted her over the issue during Tuesday night's gubernatorial debate.
Hochul instead turned the exchange toward Americans killed by federal immigration agents.

Looking directly at Hochul as he brought up several victims, Blakeman asked what she had to say to families who will "never get to sit at another Thanksgiving dinner, never be able to open their presents on their Christmas tree.
"Will you apologize to them, and will you please return Sheridan Gorman's parents' calls to talk to you about your sanctuary policy?" he said.
NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul shifted to Immigration and Customs Enforcement after Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman asked her to apologize to families who lost loved ones to illegal immigrants, including the family of Sheridan Gorman, pictured, during Tuesday’s debate. (Anna Connors/Pool/Getty Images; Sheridan G. Gorman via Instagram)

Jose Medina-Medina, an illegal immigrant from Venezuela, faces charges related to the fatal shooting of Sheridan Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student from Yorktown, New York, as she walked with friends near her campus late at night.
Her death has fueled calls for change from her parents, who have taken aim at sanctuary policies that limit cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE.
Hochul responded by calling all crimes "heartbreaking," adding, "I abhor all crimes, regardless of the perpetrator."
She went on to say her administration has spent billions to "help law enforcement do their jobs" and reduce crime across the state.
SHERIDAN GORMAN’S MOM SCORCHES DEM LAWMAKERS SHE SAYS REFUSED TO HEAR FAMILIES OF SLAIN AMERICANS
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents conduct immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis Jan. 28, 2026. (Madison Thorn/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"We have driven down crime to historic lows, especially violent crimes like shootings and murders, and that didn't come easy," she said. "That took a lot of work. I've had to change laws. I've got to allocate more money."

Hochul did not directly answer Blakeman's request for an apology or his question about returning Gorman's parents' calls. Instead, she brought up Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed during separate confrontations with federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January.
"When you're talking about ICE, what I find so shocking is that when an American mother was murdered by ICE agents, you said that her killing was justified," she fired back.
MULLIN CALLS MAMDANI'S ANTI-ICE RHETORIC 'DANGEROUS' FOLLOWING NEW YORK SHOOTING

Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman face off in the only scheduled debate ahead of the November New York gubernatorial election Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in New York. (Anna Connors/Pool The New York Times)

She said Blakeman did not have an answer when asked whether Pretti’s death was "justified," saying, "I find those answers just reprehensible, so you won't apologize. I apologize for any pain that has happened to anyone."
The exchange set off a wave of social media scrutiny, with critics accusing Hochul of not caring about the victims.
"INSANE! Kathy Hochul can’t even apologize to victims of crimes committed by illegal aliens - or promise to return their calls," RNC Research posted on X.
"She couldn't care less," radio host Brett Winterble posted on X.
"Disgusting," Republican National Committee spokesperson Kristen Cianci posted on X.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"NO APOLOGY. No ownership of the sanctuary policies," Richard Sementa, executive producer of "The Mark Levin Show," posted on X.

"BOOM! Bruce Blakeman put Kathy Hochul's immigration policies on trial, live. Bruce Blakeman: "What do you say to their families, Kathy?" Families of victims want answers, and Hochul still hasn't given them one," conservative influencer Gunther Eagleman posted on X.
Voters will decide between Hochul and Blakeman in the upcoming November election to determine who will serve as New York governor.

title: Trump scores win from liberal-leaning 9th Circuit in ICE enforcement showdown
summary: The 9th Circuit ruled the Trump administration is "certain to succeed" against California's No Vigilantes Act, dealing a blow to Gavin Newsom.
story: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law requiring major companies to search historical records and publicly disclose certain slavery-era transactions, as supporters framed the measure as a step toward accountability.

The Trump administration scored a victory at a liberal-leaning appeals court Wednesday, which temporarily blocked a section of a California law requiring plainclothes federal law enforcement agents to show their badges and identification when carrying out operations.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled the Trump administration was "certain to succeed" in its lawsuit against California, finding that the No Vigilantes Act’s identification requirement violates the Constitution’s supremacy clause, which says federal law takes priority when it conflicts with state law.
"Section 10 explicitly overrides the federal government’s power to determine whether, how, and when to publicly identify its officers," the panel wrote.

The preliminary injunction comes from a federal appeals court that has repeatedly clashed with the Trump administration over some of its signature immigration policies, including blocking efforts to withhold federal funding from sanctuary cities in 2018, restricting attempts to tighten asylum eligibility that same year and refusing to reinstate Trump's travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries in 2017.
FEDERAL COURT BLOCKS NEWSOM’S BID TO SHACKLE ICE IN TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN

Residents confront federal agents and Border Patrol agents over their presence in their neighborhood on Atlantic Boulevard in the Los Angeles suburb of Bell. California last year passed a law banning authorities from wearing masks. (Getty Images)

The ruling comes as a major blow to California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, widely viewed as a 2028 presidential hopeful. Newsom has positioned himself as a leading opponent of Trump's immigration agenda, signing a series of laws aimed at protecting immigrant communities, restricting federal immigration enforcement operations and increasing oversight of federal agents in the state.

"California is proud to fight for the safety of our communities against the federal government’s campaign of terror and weaponized incompetence," a spokesperson for Newsom's office said in a statement. "Their tactics continue to harm our families every day."

The Trump administration sued California over provisions in the No Vigilantes Act and No Secret Police Act, which restricts law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings, in November 2025. Judge Christina Snyder, a Clinton-appointed judge, initially blocked the No Secret Police Act's mask restriction for federal officers but declined to block the No Vigilantes Act's identification requirement.

The Trump administration appealed Snyder's decision on the identification requirement, and the 9th Circuit temporarily blocked its enforcement in February before granting an injunction pending appeal in April.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS

Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks after U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer granted an emergency temporary restraining order to stop President Trump's deployment of the California National Guard June 12, 2025, at the California State Supreme Court building in San Francisco. (Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)

California argued that its identification requirement did not amount to an unconstitutional regulation of the federal government because a state law crosses that line only when it "impose[s] substantial burdens on federal operations."
But the appeals court ruled that the state never had the authority to directly regulate federal officials.
"The burden of the regulation on federal operations, whether substantial or otherwise, is irrelevant," the court wrote.
The liberal appeals court ruling drew praise from Trump administration officials, including Brett Shumate, assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Division.
DOJ WARNS FORMER RED STATE IS BECOMING THE NEXT CALIFORNIA AS GOVERNOR EMBRACES ICE LIMITS
Security guards stand in front of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco June 12, 2017. (Getty Images)
"The Ninth Circuit agrees that California cannot regulate federal law enforcement," Schumate wrote on X.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Today, the Ninth Circuit again affirms what common sense makes clear: California cannot regulate how Federal law enforcement officers carry out their jobs authorized by Congress," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, Jr. wrote on X.
"Today's decision is a huge WIN for protecting the safety of our Nation's law enforcement officers and ensuring @POTUS 's promise to enforce our Nation's immigration laws," Woodward continued.

title: Trump-backed GOP candidate who ousted scandal-plagued incumbent warns against 'never-ending war' with Iran
summary: Television journalist turned congressional hopeful Ryan Elijah says transparency, accountability will be his focus following victory over Cory Mills in contentious Florida GOP primary.
story: Ryan Elijah, who defeated Rep. Cory Mills in the Republican primary, says the U.S. must prevent a nuclear-armed Iran while drawing down the military conflict.
For 14 years, Ryan Elijah reported on Central Florida’s biggest stories from the television newsroom. Now, he is on a mission to represent the same community in Congress.

Elijah stepped into a contentious GOP primary in which he warned that incumbent Cory Mills was at risk of losing the Republican-leaning district to the Democrats, following a series of personal and professional scandals.
Elijah won a convincing victory in the August 18 Republican primary, receiving 47% of the vote to Mills' 34%.
Trump, who had originally endorsed Mills, later claimed that he had privately encouraged the embattled congressman to withdraw from the race.
REP CORY MILLS DRAWS FIRST REPUBLICAN CHALLENGER AS SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS, EXPULSION THREAT MOUNT
Former local TV news anchor Ryan Elijah unseated Rep. Cory Mills in a high-stakes Florida GOP primary race. (Mike McClain/Ryan Elijah for Congress)

Recently, the veteran television journalist sat down with Fox News Digital to discuss his views on Iran, affordability, and immigration, while pledging to remain an independent voice in Congress, and a strong advocate for Volusia and Seminole counties.
Elijah did not take the decision to leave working in media lightly, but felt a call to leadership:

"I love my job. It's something I could have retired from TV and been perfectly happy. But I think we all look for the time you're asked to step up and lead. And for me, that was this time. When we saw how the primary was playing out, it just became clear that we were going to lose this election in November.

"And I decided that we had the connections in this community to throw our hat in the ring. We had the trust from the community and the primary played out a lot like we thought it would, where people wanted a choice. I think that's what primaries are all about in Seminole County and Volusia County spoke really loud. In that primary, and now I think they put us in a great spot to hold this seat in November."
Elijah pledges to put transparency and accountability front and center for the constituents of the seventh district:

"Well, I think transparency and accountability are huge issues. I think when I talk to people, they don't feel like they're heard very much in Washington. And I think that you have to be transparent about whatever you can. And first of all, if you have nothing to hide, that's the best way to be transparent because you can exactly show your business dealings and how your life dealings are.

Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., attends the House Armed Services Committee hearing titled "Department of Defense FY2027 Budget Request," in Rayburn building on Wednesday, April 29, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"And that's something we've talked about a lot…and then in terms of accountability, no one is above the law. And that's a message that Americans want to hear, whether you're a Democrat or Republican, there are laws for a reason, and we have to make sure those laws are upheld."
As the military engagement with Iran is rattling global energy markets and pinching Americans' pocketbooks, Elijah concedes the need to thwart a nuclear Iran, but also is wary of another forever war:
GOP RISING STAR HELPED TOPPLE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT. NOW HE'S CAUGHT LEADERSHIP'S EYE

"This is a decade-long issue and a conflict between Iran and its proxies, where they have targeted and they have killed Americans. So the U.S. military right now is trying to end that conflict. But as representatives, we have to listen to the American people. We have to listen to central Floridians.

"And they have been very clear on this. They're concerned about it. They are concerned this is going to be a never-ending war. They don't want that. I don't want that either. I share that belief, which is why I think we need to draw this conflict down. And we need to make sure that Iran is not a nuclear threat."

Despite previous media reporting that the Trump administration is open to allowing Iran to continue its uranium enrichment program, potentially allowing the development of Iranian nuclear weapons, President Donald Trump has taken a hardline stance on the issue, repeatedly saying he would not allow the country to develop any nuclear weapons. (Getty Images)
On the immigration issue, Elijah cites improvement under GOP leadership on the issue, but argues that enforcement focus should remain on criminals:

"This is another issue where I think you have to look at where we've come from. When you let tens of millions of illegal people into this country, you're going to have issues that take a long time to fix. And I think if you look at the way there has to be a federal, a local, and a state cooperation with immigration, that's what it takes to work. Which is why when I talk to all the sheriffs in our district that are endorsing us, they're handling immigration much better than other parts around the country because they have that cooperation.

"We need to start with the criminals. We have got many criminals still here illegally in the United States. That's what they focused on in central Florida. That's what ICE needs to focus on, removing the criminals. And there's a compassionate way to handle this as we've got an issue that is not going to be fixed in just six or 12 months."
Elijah consistently emphasizes that he will be an independent voice for the district, not a partisan rubber stamp:
"Well, I've said a lot. Look, I ran in this primary without the president's endorsement. I've been an independent voice in this and I've told a lot of people that ask me that question.

"As you can imagine, I go to a lot of doors. That's a question: ‘Will you support the president? Will you not support the president?’ And what I tell them is, if it's a policy that supports our country and supports our district, I'm going to support that policy.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent stands before a large American flag. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)
"More often than not, I will because I'm a Republican. I like a lot of those policies. If there's a policy I disagree with, we won't. So in that situation, that's where things are at."
Finally, Elijah acknowledges that affordability, while lacking a quick and easy fix, is the defining 2026 issue for much of the electorate:

"I think the number one thing that we hear from people, and that's affordability, and that's not an easy fix, but I think what they want out of government is accountability. We talked about that before, that government is going to be accountable on its spending, on its policies, and getting inflation down, which is going to lower interest rates. It's going to lower the cost of living.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"People in Central Florida, people around the country, they want to be heard. And what they're saying in a very clear tone right now is make sure that you control government spending and protect the future of our children. That's probably the biggest thing I want them to notice."
Elijah will be facing Navy veteran and former NASA employee Bale Dalton in the November 3 general election.

title: WATCH: Georgia Senate debate erupts over white supremacy allegations, Epstein ties in fiery exchange
summary: Candidates running for the US Senate in Georgia clashed over alleged neo-Nazi activity and ties to Jeffrey Epstein during their last debate before the election.
story: Sen. Jon Ossoff and Rep. Mike Collins trade accusations over alleged neo-Nazi activity linked to Collins' family and campaign donations from Jeffrey Epstein associate Reid Hoffman.

Georgia's contentious U.S. Senate race erupted into a heated confrontation Tuesday night as Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., accused GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., of allowing the dissemination of "neo-Nazi propaganda" inside his own home, prompting Collins to fire back over Ossoff's financial support from a billionaire with ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The exchange unfolded during the candidates' second and final debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election, which was hosted by the Atlanta Press Club and broadcast by Georgia Public Broadcasting network.

During the debate, Ossoff sought to tie his GOP opponent to White nationalism and repeatedly demanded that Collins commit to stopping the dissemination of hateful rhetoric involving his campaign staff, in particular Collins' son-in-law, which Ossoff alleged has continued despite blowback. Meanwhile, Collins accused his Democrat opponent of fueling threats against his family, refusing to return campaign support connected to LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and questioned Ossoff over his support for candidates linked to controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
DEM ‘EPSTEIN CLASS’ ATTACK BACKFIRES AS TOP CANDIDATES FUNDED BY EPSTEIN-TIED BILLIONAIRE
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins of Georgia speaks to supporters at a primary night event on May 19, 2026, in Jackson, Georgia. (Jason Allen/Getty Images)

"How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for the Senate?" Ossoff asked, referencing reporting about his opponent's son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, who was the subject of a CNN investigation about sharing Nazi propaganda imagery, promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories and polling his online followers about whether he should produce a video titled "Why Gen-Z Doesn't Hate Hitler."

"How about this, Mike? We can shake hands on it," Ossoff continued to press. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign, it's just three weeks, Mike, you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house? Can you make that commitment?"
Collins responded by accusing Ossoff of inflaming hostility toward his family, pointing to threats he said he and his son-in-law had received.
"I'm a little tired of this, Jon," Collins said. "There's a crazy person in jail right now because of your rhetoric," he alleged, before saying he had received another threat just the previous day.
JON OSSOFF SILENT ON SPLC INDICTMENT AFTER TAKING MORE THAN $700K FROM AFFILIATE OF INDICTED GROUP

"You have not denounced, you've not condemned Reid Hoffman, one of your largest donors out there, one that's been supporting you with over $1 million," Collins shot back. "Why don't you denounce that? Why don't you return that money?"

Collins was referring to Reid Hoffman, the billionaire LinkedIn co-founder and major Democratic donor whose past relationship with Epstein has drawn scrutiny. Hoffman has acknowledged meeting with Epstein after the financier's 2008 conviction for sex offenses and visiting his private island. Hoffman also contributed $7,000 directly to Ossoff's campaign and $1 million to a political action committee supporting the Georgia Democrat, according to previously reported campaign finance records.

Billionaire Reid Hoffman (left), a known former associate of Jeffrey Epstein, made contributions to the campaign for Sen. Jon Ossoff (right), D-Ga., and to a PAC opposing Ossoff's challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Ben Hendren/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Earlier in the debate, Collins went further, accusing Hoffman of sending Epstein ice cream with a message referencing girls, while again pressing Ossoff to reject his financial support.

"Jon Ossoff, his number one donor, one of his largest donors, is Reid Hoffman, the same guy that's in the same files, the same guy that sent ice cream, ice cream to Jeffrey Epstein on his birthday and said, 'This is for the girls,'" Collins said during an earlier exchange in the debate.
THUNE-ALIGNED GROUPS UNLEASH HISTORIC WAR CHEST TO DEFEND SENATE MAJORITY: 'WINNING MESSAGE'

The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Hoffman sent Epstein ice cream in 2014 with a message indicating it was intended for him or "for the girls." Hoffman has apologized for his association with Epstein, which he said stemmed from fundraising activities involving the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and has not been accused of wrongdoing in connection with Epstein's crimes.
Ossoff rejected the Hoffman comparison, however, arguing that the allegations against Collins involved someone living in the congressman's home rather than a political donor.

"Mike, if any of these folks were based in my house, then I'd understand you to ask me to take responsibility for them," Ossoff said. "What I asked you, Mike, was, can you commit for just three weeks to stop the production of neo-Nazi propaganda from your home?"
Earlier in the debate, Collins was directly questioned about concerns from Black Georgians over allegations of White-nationalist ties involving members of his political operation.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I condemn any sort of hate speech, antisemitism, hate of any kind. It's abhorrent," Collins responded, adding that he had fired staffers when controversies arose.

Collins also sought to turn the accusations back on Ossoff by criticizing his support for Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and invoking left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who Collins blasted for saying the U.S. deserved 9/11, and promoting anti-Semitism.

Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., condemned Hasan Piker's latest remarks about antisemitism and American Jews' support for Israel. (Ben Hendren/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"He hangs his hat on this Abdul El-Sayed, you know, the guy that hates Israel — best friends with Hasan Piker, who said that America deserves 9/11," Collins said Tuesday night.

Ossoff has previously condemned Piker's rhetoric, telling The Atlanta Journal-Constitution through a spokesperson that he "unreservedly rejects reckless and dangerous rhetoric" suggesting political advocacy justifies violence against Jewish Americans or any other community.

title: Sleeper GOP candidate puts blue-leaning state in play as fraud scandal shadows Dems
summary: Michele Tafoya trails Peggy Flanagan by just four points as Minnesota's massive welfare fraud scandal reshapes the rare GOP Senate pickup bid.
story: Republican Senate nominee in Minnesota Michele Tafoya, in a Fox News Digital interview, targets Democratic rival Peggy Flanagan's record, says voters are 'angry' over fraud scandals

Republicans are eyeing a rare Senate pickup opportunity in Minnesota, where GOP nominee Michele Tafoya is narrowing the gap with Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, prompting Fox News to move the race toward Republicans less than three weeks before Election Day.

It's been nearly a quarter-century since Republicans last won a Senate election in the blue-leaning state. But Tafoya, a former longtime NFL sideline reporter, is aiming to break that losing streak by flipping the seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith.

A new Minnesota Star Tribune/KARE 11 poll shows Tafoya trailing Flanagan by just four percentage points. On Tuesday, the Fox News Power Rankings shifted the race to the right, from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat.
GOP SENATE HOPEFUL SOUNDS ALARM AFTER TERROR PLOT THWARTED

Michele Tafoya makes her case as the GOP's Senate nominee at the Minnesota Republican state convention at the Duluth Entertainment Convention Center in Duluth, Minn., May 29, 2026. (Star Tribune via Getty Images)

"The more that Minnesotans learn about me and my opponent and see what my opponent has failed to do over the last eight years alongside [Democratic Gov.] Tim Walz, they're understanding Minnesota needs change. We need fresh ideas, we need an independent thinker and they're jumping on board," Tafoya said in a Fox News Digital interview.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Flanagan campaign for comment but didn't receive a response at the time this story was published.

The race is unfolding against the backdrop of Minnesota's massive welfare assistance fraud scandal, which has attracted national attention for nearly a year and prompted Democratic Gov. Tim Walz to abandon his 2026 re-election bid. The scandal has also become a central issue in Tafoya's campaign against Flanagan.

Tafoya noted that "there has been historic fraud under this administration, where Peggy Flanagan, my opponent, has been the second-in-charge in this state. And not only was the money stolen, it hollowed out these programs that were supposed to be getting help, like kids' meals or autistic kids or seniors who were supposed to be getting visits, health visits, wellness visits. And, so, that's been hollowed out.
DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic Senate nominee, speaks during a primary election night party Aug. 11, 2026 in Minneapolis. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)

"Walz understood that he was not going to win another term as governor with these conditions, but my opponent thinks she deserves a promotion. I think people are starting to realize she deserves a pink slip."

Flanagan has said she is "incredibly angry with the fraud," has acknowledged public frustration over the scandal and said more could have been done sooner to catch and prevent the fraud. The lieutenant governor has noted that she was not in charge of the state agencies at the center of the scandals or steering the daily state response. She has also distanced herself from Walz, who has accepted blame for the fraud.
DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT

"It's wall-to-wall coverage on every nightly news program here for months and months. We're seeing it in polling," Minnesota-based veteran national Republican strategist Kirsten Kukowski told Fox News Digital.
Pointing to Flanagan, Kukowski said she has "a lot of fraud baggage ... and it's really made the Senate race really tight here."
Tafoya is also highlighting a recent spate of gang-related shootings in the Minneapolis-St. Paul suburbs and on Monday announced a five-point-plan to combat the violence.
"We will do more in our first eight weeks as a U.S. Senator than Peggy Flanagan has done in eight years as the second in charge," she told Fox News Digital.
WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POWER RANKINGS

"First of all, we've got to name the problem, and even Somali lawmakers and law enforcement have named this problem. We have a Somali gang violence problem. We've got to name it. She refuses to name it. You can't fix it if you don't name it," Tafoya emphasized as she referred to Flanagan.

Flanagan, a progressive candidate backed by left-wing champions, Sens. Bernie Sanders Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Ro Khanna, topped more moderate Democratic Rep. Angie Craig by roughly 20 points in the August Senate primary.

Tafoya grabbed over 50% of the vote in the GOP Senate primary as she topped a crowded field of rivals. She was heavily recruited by national Republicans, including Sen. Tim Scott, the National Republican Senatorial Committee chair.
"We did a really good job of recruiting the most independent-minded Republican who understands why it's important to win in Minnesota," Scott said in an interview on Fox News' "Hannity."
"Michele Tafoya has a story to tell. She's doing a really good job. This is a race that will come down to the wire."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Fox News Power Rankings Senate forecast (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, the top Republican in the chamber, recently teamed up on the campaign trail in Minnesota with Tafoya. But the Thune-aligned Senate Leadership Fund, the top super PAC backing GOP Senate candidates, has yet to make a major investment in the race.

Asked about national Republican support, Tafoya said, "We are getting small dollar donations from all over the country. We're getting donations from every county in this state, and I am a happy warrior. And I will deal with the circumstances I'm given. ... We're going to win this campaign on ideas."
Democrats are hopeful that popular Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who is running for governor this year, may help push Flanagan over the finish line.

"Our latest poll has Flanagan with a strong lead, and we fully expect her to be elected to the U.S. Senate," Lauren French, communications director for the Senate Democrat-aligned Senate Majority PAC, told Fox News Digital.

French argued that "Republicans are spending in deep red states and watching the battleground map extend around them. Their desperate last-minute attempt to push Minnesota into play is a political ploy."
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Michele Tafoya, left, says Peggy Flanagan, right, represents a shift toward "Democrat socialism" in Minnesota. (Fox News Digital ; Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)
Flanagan has repeatedly tied Tafoya to President Donald Trump, whose approval ratings are well underwater in Minnesota.
"Michele Tafoya is all in for Donald Trump — and he's all in for her," Flanagan reiterated Monday in a social media post.

Flanagan, who is Native American, also wrote on X, "My Ojibwe name is Gizhiiwewidamookwe, which means ‘Speaks in a Loud and Clear Voice Woman.’ I’m going to be Minnesota’s voice in the U.S. Senate — not Donald Trump’s."
But Tafoya appears to be putting some daylight between herself and Trump, as she highlights her support for abortion rights.

"I’m a pro-choice Republican not afraid to stand up to my party," Tafoya says in a new campaign commercial. "When Trump is right, I will work with him. When he is wrong, I will stand up for Minnesota."
The ad was quickly criticized by leaders on the right.

title: Dem AG's election crusade against Trump runs into embarrassing dead-felon blunder back home
summary: Jay Jones launched a Voter Protection unit targeting Trump's election security efforts, but critics point to dead felons receiving voting rights letters.
story: DOJ indictments target alleged non-citizen voter fraud in Minnesota as Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the charges. McCotter reveals that federal prosecutors have charged 50 individuals with voting crimes over the past month. The DOJ is also appealing a Florida federal judge's ruling that declared a federal law banning non-citizen voting unconstitutional.

President Donald Trump and his election security efforts were a central target in Virginia Democratic Attorney General Jay Jones' rollout of a "Voter Protection" unit, but Republican critics say the announcement overlooked voting- rights controversies unfolding in his own backyard.

Jones formed the Voter Protection Section on Tuesday to enforce state voting-rights laws as Virginia faces scrutiny over restoration letters sent to deceased felons amid Gov. Abigail Spanberger's restoration of voting rights to more than 66,000 Virginians.

Jones "launched this section to address the continued erosion of the federal Voting Rights Act, Donald Trump’s relentless attacks on our democracy, and his administration's efforts to impede access to the ballot," his office said in a statement.
TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS

Jones' announcement did not identify specific Trump administration actions, but the president signed a March 2025 order seeking stricter proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registration and changes to mail-ballot rules and backed the SAVE Act to mandate voter ID.

"At a time when the Trump administration has sought to push the federal government further into the administration of state elections, we will work closely with the Department of Elections and the Federal Accountability Unit to protect Virginia’s authority, the integrity of our elections, and every eligible voter’s right to be heard," said Ajay Saini, the OAG official Jones named to lead the division.
However, critics quickly faulted the unit for overlooking controversies within Virginia's own government after the felon rights-restoration scandal broke earlier this month.

"‘Two Bullets’ Jay Jones is now worried about ‘misinformation’ after just this year telling Virginians that Democrats’ illegal gerrymandering power grab was about ‘fairness’," the Republican Party of Virginia (RPV) said in a statement, referencing Jones’ previous reported text messages envisioning shooting a prior GOP House speaker twice instead of former German Chancellor Adolf Hitler or Cambodian dictator Pol Pot.
TRUMP ELECTION INTEGRITY PUSH EXPOSES MASSIVE AMOUNT OF DEAD PEOPLE ON NORTH CAROLINA VOTER ROLLS
Virginia attorney general candidate Jerrauld "Jay" Jones speaks at an event in Norfolk, Virginia, on June 17, 2025. (Trevor Metcalfe/The Virginian-Pilot/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

"The top priority for this new division should be finding out how many dead felons have had their rights restored, and how that happened in the first place," current Virginia House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Gate City, told Fox News Digital.

Several Virginians reported receiving restoration notices addressed to deceased relatives. Fredericksburg resident Howard Lambert confirmed to Fox News Digital a letter addressed to his late daughter indicated officials had reviewed her case before restoring her rights.
34,000 DEAD PEOPLE FOUND ON VOTER ROLLS PROMPTS EXPERT TO SLAM DEMS FOR RESISTING 'COMMONSENSE' CLEANUP

Kim Taylor, a former Republican delegate from the Petersburg area, told Fox News Digital on Wednesday that Jones' pledge to protect Virginians’ votes ignores his silence on both the "dead felons" scandal and a Democrat-supported November ballot measure that would take restoration rights away from the governor and automatically empower formerly incarcerated felons to vote.

"Jay Jones can create all the fancy new ‘voter protection’ units he wants to make himself feel better, but it’s nothing more than an empty political gesture when Richmond is mailing voting rights restoration letters to dead felons," Taylor said.
VIRGINIA SUPREME COURT TOSSES DEM-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP, UPENDING EXPECTED 10–1 EDGE
Virginia AG Jay Jones, left, embraces Gov. Abigail Spanberger, during 2026 inaugural ceremonies in Richmond. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

"With three critical constitutional amendments on the ballot, including one fundamentally changing felon voting rights, Virginians need real election integrity instead of another taxpayer-funded political stunt."

The White House also hammered Jones on Wednesday, with spokeswoman Lauren Bis telling Fox News Digital that "radical Virginia Democrats, like Jay Jones, love to preach about ‘protecting our elections’ while mailing ballots to dead felons."

"This is nothing more than a political stunt, while President Trump is fighting every day to ensure that only American citizens elect American leaders and to enact commonsense measures like voter ID."
When pressed on those issues and on Republicans’ claims that the SAVE Act provides protections itself, a spokesperson for Jones declined to elaborate beyond an initial statement:

"I was raised by people who understood that the right to vote was never simply given. Generations of Americans had to sacrifice, organize, and show extraordinary courage to claim that right," Jones said. "That history is personal to me, and it reminds us that the work of civil rights and voting rights is never finished."

"That is why we created a dedicated Voter Protection Section within the Office of the Attorney General. This work now has a permanent home, and a team focused every day on defending voting rights and enforcing Virginia law," he added, calling protection of voting rights a "year-round" responsibility.

Virginia Beach attorney Tim Anderson, who has focused on Richmond’s legal maneuvers regarding both immigration enforcement and voting rights, said Tuesday that Jones’ plan raises a separate question about enforcement against noncitizens who vote illegally amid Virginia's restricted cooperation with DHS.

Anderson previously discussed the dead-felons case with Fox News Digital and noted Tuesday that Gov. Abigail Spanberger previously restricted ICE’s use of public property, including through guidance involving encounters at polls.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
President Trump juxtaposed next to Jay Jones, Democratic nominee for Virginia Attorney General. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images; Mike Kropf/Richmond Times-Dispatch via AP, Pool)

"Now Attorney General Jay Jones says his office will enforce Virginia’s election laws. Then answer this, Attorney General: Does that include prosecuting noncitizens who knowingly vote illegally—with the same enthusiasm you bring to protecting access to the polls? We know this is a big fat ‘No’. Enforce the whole law," he said.

The Democratic Party of Virginia, however, backed Jones’ new unit, arguing that Trump is "attacking voting rights [and] Virginia is not backing down," as election security remains a prominent issue heading into the midterms.

title: Mamdani accuses Blakeman of 'bigotry and racism' in breakout debate that mayor didn't watch
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani admitted he didn't watch Tuesday's gubernatorial debate between Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican Bruce Blakeman.
story: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman of spreading ‘bigotry and racism’ in a debate against Gov. Kathy Hochul.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman of "bigotry and racism" Tuesday night despite admitting he didn't watch Blakeman's debate with Gov. Kathy Hochul live.

Mamdani made the statement in comments to reporters Wednesday after Blakeman and Hochul squared off Tuesday night. A reporter asked Mamdani whether he was bothered that Hochul hadn't responded to Blakeman's claims that the NYC mayor is an antisemite.

"So, I think, you know, it is hard for anyone to keep up with all of the bigotry and racism that Bruce Blakeman exhibits on a regular basis. So, I think that the governor did a good job. And I'll never fault someone for not being able to catch all of it because that is a fool's errand when it comes to Bruce Blakeman," Mamdani said.
SHOCK POLL: POWERFUL BLUE STATE GOV'S LEAD SHRINKS TO SINGLE DIGITS WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION

Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman face off in the only scheduled debate ahead of the November New York gubernatorial election Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in New York. (Anna Connors/Pool The New York Times)

"And I think the governor also made clear, you know, I've said that I, I didn't watch the debate beyond the clip, but I think the governor has made clear time and time again what her vision is. It's a vision of a more affordable New York," he continued.

"And when it comes to Bruce Blakeman, his vision seems to be making life harder for working people. When the governor and I announced putting our city on a pathway to universal childcare, Bruce Blakeman went on television and said this was rewarding lazy parents who would sit at home and watch 'The View.' When we were speaking about concerns about what HR1 was going to do with regards to healthcare access across the state, Bruce Blakeman went on television and said that he would cut Medicaid in half."

The debate opened with the candidates being asked about the conduct of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which last week drew outrage in New York City after the shooting of a 28-year-old Dominican national whom the Department of Homeland Security said refused to comply with lawful orders during a targeted operation in the Bronx. A 5-year-old boy inside Oscar Bergal's vehicle was unharmed.
New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman (Getty Images; Fox News composite)

"Kathy Hochul appealed to ICE to let this criminal out. The question that New Yorkers have to ask is what was this guy doing in New York in the first place? It's because Kathy Hochul has made us a sanctuary state," Blakeman said.
MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION'

"Think about it. This guy came into the country illegally. He's been convicted of a crime. He's got pending charges for dealing drugs, poison to our children. And he's a gang banger. This is who Kathy Hochul is defending?" Blakeman continued.

"I have a cooperative agreement with ICE until Kathy Hochul said we could no longer cooperate with ICE. We got over 2,000 illegal migrants out of my county with criminal records ranging from rape, attempted murder, robbery, burglary, drug dealing, carjacking, gang activity.

"And that's because we cooperated with ICE, and we didn't raid one school, one hospital, one daycare center or one church. If you cooperate with federal law enforcement, it makes for a safer community. That's what I did. Kathy Hochul is taking that ability away from us. That's why things like this happen."
Hochul called Blakeman's response a "non-answer" because "he refused to condemn what ICE did."
MULLIN CALLS MAMDANI'S ANTI-ICE RHETORIC 'DANGEROUS' FOLLOWING NEW YORK SHOOTING

"So, he basically says in the state of New York, he'd be fine if ICE agents shoot into cars, shoot guns into vehicles, not knowing who's inside and could have killed a 5-year-old child. If that doesn't shock the conscience of everybody — and it should shock his conscience as well — that he says, 'That's OK, that's how ICE is supposed to do it,'" Hochul added.

"I'll tell you what. I oversee over 500 policing agencies in the state of New York. Over half a million arrests every year. That's not how you conduct yourself. ICE is out of control. It's out of control in Nassau County."
New York Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman and New York Governor Kathy Hochul  (Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images; Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Blakeman pushed back, saying, "It never would have happened" but for Hochul's "sanctuary policy."
Fox News' Greg Norman contributed to this report.

title: Hochul deflects when pressed on ties to 'anti-Christian' Mamdani in fiery debate moment: 'Shame on you'
summary: New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul was pressed on her endorsement of Mayor Zohran Mamdani after Bruce Blakeman called him an antisemite.
story: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman sparred over her support for NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a contentious debate Tuesday night.

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul declined to directly defend socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during Tuesday night's gubernatorial debate after her Republican challenger accused him of being antisemitic, anti-Christian and un-American.

"With all the issues that face New York City, the first thing he did was sign an executive order to water down the definition of antisemitism, shame on you, mayor," Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman said on the debate stage before pointing his attention at Hochul over her endorsement of the socialist New York City mayor.

"You are campaigning around the state with a guy who doesn't believe in American values," Blakeman said. "He talks about collectivism. That means you take personal property rights away. You take other people's property rights. This is a guy that's anti-Christian, couldn't find an hour out of his day to attend the installation of a new archbishop here in New York City, the biggest religion in the city of New York. Look, if you want to campaign with him, that's fine. But I will tell you right now, I think Zohran Mamdani is an antisemite. I believe he's anti-Christian. And I don't think he has American values."

Hochul responded by turning to the moderator and deciding to answer a previous question about comments, reported by the New York Times, Blakeman made in a "secret meeting" related to whether the NYPD under Mamdani would respond if far-left protesters were causing violence against the Jewish community. Blakeman disputed her characterization of that meeting before complimenting Mamdani for selecting and keeping Jessica Tisch as NYPD commissioner.
"Let's move on," the moderator then said.
SCHUMER, JEFFRIES DODGE MAMDANI CONTROVERSY AS FELLOW NEW YORK DEM UNLOADS

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman sparred over a variety of issues in their first and only debate, including NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani (Anna Connors - Pool/Getty Images; John Nacion/Getty Images for Empire State Realty Trust)
"Antisemitism is on the rise, and it's occurred under your watch, and Zohran Mamdani is fueling it," Blakeman added before the conversation moved to another topic.
Republicans quickly highlighted the exchange on social media.
HOCHUL'S OFFICE MOCKS KATIE ZACHARIA WITH AARON RODGERS INJURY POST DESPITE GOVERNOR'S PRESS SECRETARY SCANDAL

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at the site where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during an operation in the Bronx, on October 8, 2026, in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

"Zohran Mamdani is an antisemite, he’s anti-Christian, and he’s anti-American. And Kathy Hochul is campaigning with him," Kristin Cianci, Northeast Comms Director for the Republican National Committee (RNC) posted on X. "What an utter disgrace. New York deserves better."
"Zohran Mamdani is an antisemite, anti-Christian and anti-American," the New York Republican Party posted on X. "And he's Kathy Hochul's best friend. "

Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman face off in the only scheduled debate ahead of the November New York gubernatorial election on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in New York. (Anna Connors/Pool The New York Times)

Hochul was asked about the exchange and why she "didn't defend the mayor" by a reporter on Wednesday morning during a press conference on the state's investment into the first-ever community center in Jackson Heights.
"I’m not going to take the bait from someone who’s throwing out such insane arguments," Hochul said.

"He had a litany of things that were either false or so absurd that I’m not going to dignify them with a response from me, the governor. So, everyone knows I reject that, his description of the mayor. The mayor and I are great partners, we’re working hard together. And I’m not gonna give him the dignity of responding to those kind of crazy comments. And that’s pretty consistent how I’ve been."
The two New York politicians clashed on a variety of issues on Tuesday night, including President Donald Trump, a recent ICE-involved shooting, energy prices, and inflation.
Democrats outnumber Republicans by a roughly two-to-one margin in blue-leaning New York state, but polling in September indicated that Blakeman has cut his deficit against Hochul to single digits.

Hochul, who is running for a second full four-year term steering the nation's fourth most populous state, stood at 50% support among likely voters in New York, with Blakeman at 41%, according to a Siena College poll conducted Sept. 11-17.
By a 50%-30% margin, voters said Mamdani's support for Hochul is a plus for the governor's bid for re-election.

title: Man posing as NFL player accused of conning women out of $1.3M
summary: Domonique DuBose spotted red flags when a man on Hinge with 85,000 followers and a blue checkmark claimed to be a San Francisco 49ers player.
story: A man claiming to play for the San Francisco 49ers matched with a woman on a dating app, but Domonique DuBose had her doubts. When DuBose joined The CyberGuy Report podcast, she explained how she became suspicious of a man who allegedly used a fake NFL identity to pursue women and promote fraudulent investments.

A man claiming to play for the San Francisco 49ers matches with you on a dating app. His Instagram has 85,000 followers and a blue checkmark. There are videos showing what appears to be his football lifestyle. He drives luxury cars and seems to have plenty of money. So, would you believe him?

Domonique DuBose had her doubts. When she joined me on The CyberGuy Report podcast, she explained how she became suspicious of a man who allegedly used a fake NFL identity to pursue women and promote fraudulent investments. Federal prosecutors say Daejon Labrayae Love and an alleged accomplice received approximately $1.3 million from at least 26 women.

Love pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a felony charge of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and a public defender representing him did not reply to a request for comment. Magistrate Judge Jolie A. Russo ordered Love detained as a flight risk.

DuBose recognized warning signs and avoided losing any money herself. "Basically, I caught on right away," DuBose told me. What she uncovered raises serious questions about how easily someone can fake an identity online and how you can spot the warning signs before it's too late.

‘TINDER SWINDLER’ ROMANCE FRAUDSTER PROMISES ‘SAFE’ DATING APP – USING INTEL FROM CON MAN PLAYBOOK

According to an FBI affidavit, investigators allege Daejon Love used football-related imagery to support claims that he was a 49ers player, while representatives of the team and NFL said he had never been employed by either organization. (FBI via court documents)
How the fake 49ers player made his story believable

According to DuBose, Love's Instagram account looked like something you might expect from a professional athlete. His posts showed him wearing San Francisco 49ers clothing and enjoying an expensive lifestyle. There were also videos from football-related locations, including footage that appeared connected to the Super Bowl in New Orleans.
"It looked valid. I mean, he had 85,000 followers. He had a blue check," DuBose recalled. She even contacted a friend who had played for the 49ers.

Surprisingly, she says that friend initially supported Love's story. Still, she continued investigating. "I looked at everything from the NFL roster for the Niners to IR to practice squad," she explained.

She also searched his college football history, looking for evidence that he had actually played at the professional level. Another detail bothered her. Nearly every photo seemed to feature 49ers clothing. To DuBose, who knew professional football players, that constant display of team merchandise seemed unusual. Federal investigators later confirmed with representatives of the NFL and the 49ers that Love had never been employed by either organization. That's what makes this case so troubling. A convincing social media profile can make someone seem credible long before anyone checks the facts behind it.
The dating app red flags that caught her attention
DuBose said she met Love on Hinge. His profile described him as an NFL receiver, but their first interactions made her uncomfortable. "It was really fast how he wanted to get my number," she told me.

Instead of sharing her personal number, she took a precaution that limited how much information he could access. "I gave him my work cell phone number instead of my own phone number, and he started texting me."

Then came an unusual flood of attention. Love sent several videos and voice recordings almost immediately. One recording played during our podcast interview included this opening: "So what's up, beautiful? I had to shoot my shot with you." The messages also included extravagant claims about his wealth and how much he wanted to spend time with her. For DuBose, the pace of the attention felt strange. "And it was just so fast. It was so rapid," she recalled.

Some of his other claims raised even more questions. DuBose said he talked about coming from a wealthy Swiss family and having ownership interests involving Gucci stores. She struggled to reconcile those stories with his supposed NFL career. Rather than accepting the explanation, she kept checking.
The many identities behind the alleged $1.3 million scam

Love's supposed football career was only one part of the alleged operation. During our podcast conversation, I asked DuBose about his different identities. She explained that he appeared to have more than two, with different names and professional backgrounds depending on whom he approached. According to federal investigators, Love used several names, including Jon Love, Daejon Love, Avril Lyto Love and Jordan Love. His professional identity also changed depending on the person he approached. "He was a real estate investor. He was a day trader," DuBose explained.

Prosecutors say Love used those claims to convince women that he had access to lucrative investment opportunities. His alleged accomplice, Taylor Jamie Chan, posed as a financial advisor who helped manage Love's fortune, court records allege. Together, they allegedly used fake bank and investment accounts showing enormous balances. They also staged FaceTime calls displaying fabricated investment gains. Some women even took out personal loans after Love promised they would quickly be repaid, the affidavit says.
READ THE AFFIDAVIT – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

DuBose told me that some women appeared to receive early investment returns, which encouraged them to invest more. However, federal investigators say none of the victims they interviewed reported receiving actual returns after sending money. When women ran out of money or started asking too many questions, prosecutors allege Love cut off contact.
An FBI affidavit details how Daejon Labrayae Love allegedly used a fake 49ers persona, custom helmets and prop money to defraud 26 women of $1.3M. (Getty Images)
More women come forward in the fake NFL player case

The federal investigation has grown since the arrests. On Sept. 18, the FBI reported that 35 additional women had come forward claiming they were defrauded. Investigators were still working to verify those allegations. If confirmed, the number of identified victims would rise from 26 to 61. For DuBose, the emotional damage described by women who say they encountered Love has been particularly painful. She told me that some women described relationships lasting years. Others said they became deeply involved with someone whose identity they never fully understood. "There's some that dated him for 11, 12, 13 years off and on," she said.

Those longer timelines reflect what women reportedly told DuBose. They extend beyond the February 2022 start date of the alleged financial scheme documented by federal investigators. "It breaks my heart," she told me during our interview. She was especially disturbed by the emotional vulnerability that someone could exploit when a person believes a relationship is genuine. "And using that to your advantage is just sick."

DuBose also told me that she would like to confront Love about his alleged actions. After hearing so many stories, there's one answer she still wants. "I want to know why." The FBI has encouraged potential victims to come forward, even if they feel embarrassed about what happened. Investigators say reports from additional people may help them understand the full scope of the alleged scheme.
Can dating apps do more to stop fake identities?

One of the biggest questions raised by this case involves the platforms where these relationships begin. A blue checkmark and a large online following can make an account appear trustworthy. However, verification features vary by platform, and confirming an account holder's identity does not establish that their claimed career or wealth is genuine. DuBose expressed frustration about how easily someone can construct a false life on dating apps. "As far as the dating apps go, you can be whoever you want on those dating apps. And that's the scary part."

She acknowledged that some platforms offer identity checks. However, she questioned whether those checks could ever guarantee that someone was telling the truth about their background. That's a concern worth considering. A person can use their real name and still make false claims about their job. They can also provide authentic photographs while exaggerating their wealth. For anyone meeting a stranger online, independent verification remains an important safeguard.
LUTHER DAVIS ALLEGEDLY WORE DISGUISES TO POSE AS NFL PLAYERS IN MULTI-MILLION DOLLAR LOAN FRAUD SCHEME
How to protect yourself from fake dating profiles
You can still meet people online while taking precautions against fraud. These steps can help you identify suspicious behavior before a relationship becomes financially risky.

If someone says they play professional sports or hold a prestigious position, check official organizational records. Don't rely on social media search results alone. For example, NFL teams publish player rosters that you can check against someone's claims.

Excessive attention early in a conversation may be an attempt to establish trust before introducing a financial request. Pay attention if someone immediately wants to move off the dating app or begins discussing a serious relationship before you've had time to get acquainted.
There are precautions you can take against fraud when meeting someone on a dating app. (Alicia Windzio/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Communicate through the dating app until you feel comfortable. A separate phone number can help limit exposure, although it won't eliminate every risk. Avoid sharing your home address or workplace details with someone you have only recently met online.

Look for inconsistent names or multiple profiles using the same images. A reverse image search may reveal whether someone has copied photographs from another person's account. Our CyberGuy article explains how to avoid dating app scammers.

Be especially skeptical of guaranteed returns or requests to take out personal loans. Independently check any financial opportunity before considering it. Someone who genuinely cares about you should respect your decision to keep your finances separate.

Conflicting information about someone's background deserves a closer look. Give yourself time to verify details without pressure. If the person becomes defensive or tries to discourage you from checking their claims, consider that another warning sign. DuBose continues taking precautions when meeting new people. She told me that she checks phone numbers and tries to establish whether someone is using a legitimate identity. "If you text me the moment you text me, I'm reverse checking your number. I'm making sure your name is valid." A reverse lookup can provide useful clues, although scammers may use spoofed numbers or accounts registered under other people's names.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
What to do if you already sent money to a scammer
If you suspect someone has deceived you through a dating app, act quickly. Your chances of recovering money may depend on how you paid and how soon you report the transaction.

Explain what happened and ask whether it can reverse or recall the payment. If you sent money through a wire transfer or payment app, contact that service's fraud department as soon as possible. Speed can be important when attempting to recover funds.

Save screenshots of messages and dating profiles. Keep financial transaction records that could help investigators. Don't delete conversations before documenting them, even if the experience is upsetting.

An Instagram account associated with Daejon Love displayed San Francisco 49ers gear and luxury vehicles, helping support his alleged false identity as an NFL player. (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon)

File a complaint through IC3.gov and provide as much information as possible. Include the person's usernames, phone numbers and payment details. You can also report suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Report the suspicious account so the platform can investigate and take appropriate action. Include any evidence showing that the person misrepresented their identity or requested money.

Criminals sometimes contact fraud victims again, claiming they can retrieve stolen money in exchange for an upfront payment. Be skeptical of anyone promising guaranteed recovery, especially if they request additional payments or sensitive financial information. If you have information involving Daejon Love or Taylor Chan specifically, the FBI requests tips through tips.fbi.gov or 1-800-CALL-FBI.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stayed with me after speaking with Domonique DuBose on The CyberGuy Report podcast was how convincing this alleged deception became. We're talking about someone who reportedly built an entire lifestyle around a career he never had. He used the credibility of a major NFL team and social media to get people to believe him. Some allegedly trusted him with significant amounts of money. During our conversation, I raised a question that I think deserves a serious answer. These social media companies can collect an extraordinary amount of information about us. As I put it on the podcast, "these social media companies know what toothbrush we're using and when we're going to buy a loaf of bread." So why does it remain so difficult to identify someone who builds a false professional identity and uses it to target people? I also admire how thoroughly DuBose investigated the situation. Even when someone she knew appeared to validate the story, she continued asking questions. Her experience is a reminder that you should never feel pressured to trust someone simply because their online life looks convincing.

If a dating app verifies someone's identity but that person turns out to be lying about who they are, should the platform share responsibility for the damage? Or do you believe people should be entirely responsible for protecting themselves? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

A smartphone can share location and other device data that may reveal sensitive details about where you go. (Tero Vesalainen/Getty Images)
Your phone can carry an advertising identifier

Smartphones can use advertising identifiers that help advertisers and developers measure ads and activity. On Apple devices, the system advertising identifier is known as the IDFA. Android devices can use Google's advertising ID.

Advertising identifiers can help connect activity across apps when apps and advertising systems are permitted to use them. Combined with location data and other signals, those identifiers can help companies build a much more detailed trail of where a device has been.

And a trail stops being anonymous fast. A device that sleeps at your address every night and turns up at a dialysis center every Tuesday and Thursday isn't much of a mystery to anyone who can connect those locations with other identifying information.
The apps hand it off, and it keeps moving

An app asks for your location. Often for a fair reason, like providing a local forecast or showing the nearest pharmacy. What many people don't realize is that apps can include advertising and analytics software from outside companies. Depending on the app, its permissions and its privacy practices, that technology may collect or receive information about your device and location. Location information can also become part of the digital advertising ecosystem, where information about a device can pass among multiple companies. Once location data leaves your phone, controlling where it goes next becomes much harder.
Federal regulators have already gone after this

This isn't a theory about what could happen. The government spent years fighting one such case in court. On May 4, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission announced a settlement that bars the data broker Kochava and its subsidiary, Collective Data Solutions, from selling, sharing or disclosing sensitive location data without people's affirmative express consent, subject to the terms of the order. The FTC alleged Kochava sold location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices that could track people to health facilities, places of worship and other sensitive locations. Kochava did not admit wrongdoing. Kochava wasn't alone. In December 2024, the FTC took action against two more location data companies, Gravy Analytics and Mobilewalla, over allegations involving the sale of sensitive location data.
Then one of them got robbed

In January 2025, Gravy Analytics was breached. A hacker posted what they claimed was 17 terabytes of stolen data on a Russian cybercrime forum. Security researchers examining a sample found more than 30 million location points, including phones at the White House, the Kremlin and military bases around the world. The data reportedly came from everyday apps, including games and dating apps. Think about what that means. A company collects movements. Regulators take action over how sensitive location data gets handled. Then criminals allegedly obtain a massive collection of data anyway.
What your movements actually tell a stranger
Strip out the technical language. A few weeks of location data can potentially reveal:

Which clinic you go to and how often you go backWhich house of worship you attend and whether you still doWhether anyone else appears to live at your addressWhat hours your home may sit emptyWhich relatives you visit and on what day
Which clinic you go to and how often you go back
Which house of worship you attend and whether you still do
Whether anyone else appears to live at your address
What hours your home may sit empty
Which relatives you visit and on what day

Those last few can turn a privacy problem into a safety concern. A device that regularly leaves a home at the same time and returns two hours later can reveal patterns about when someone may be away. Location information can also make a scam call more convincing. "I'm calling from the billing office at the clinic on Oak Street about your visit last week" is much harder to dismiss when the clinic and timing happen to be correct. And with Medicare Open Enrollment beginning October 15, a caller who seems to know your doctor or pharmacy may sound more convincing than a random scammer.
'But I never share my location'

If you've ever tapped "Allow" on a weather app, a store app or a game, you may have shared it. You might have granted that permission years ago and forgotten about it. Even apps without precise location permission may be able to estimate your general area through information such as your internet connection. You can't make yourself invisible, but you can make your movements harder to track.
What you can do about it

You can't stop your phone from knowing where you are and still use every location-based feature. But you can limit which apps get that information and reduce some of the identifiers used for advertising and tracking. None of this takes technical skill, and you can tackle one part at a time.
Start here: limit advertising tracking
Advertising identifiers aren't the only way companies can recognize a device, but limiting them can remove one tool used to connect activity for advertising purposes.
First, control whether apps can request permission to track you across other companies' apps and websites:
Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap TrackingTurn off Allow Apps to Request to Track
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Tracking
Turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track
When this setting is off, apps that request permission to track are treated as though you selected Ask App Not to Track. They cannot access Apple's system advertising identifier, known as the IDFA.
Apple also has a separate setting for ads that Apple itself delivers:
Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap Apple AdvertisingTurn off Personalized Ads
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Apple Advertising
Turn off Personalized Ads
This second setting limits how Apple personalizes the ads it delivers in services such as the App Store, Apple News and Stocks. It is separate from the app-tracking control above.
THE SCAMMER AT YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE MAY ALREADY KNOW WHO YOU ARE
Social media apps collect more data than many users realize, from clicks and contacts to location history. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
To check your advertising ID controls:
Open SettingsTap Security and privacyScroll down and tap More privacy settingsOpen AdsTap Delete advertising ID if that option appearsConfirm your choice
Open Settings
Tap Security and privacy
Scroll down and tap More privacy settings
Open Ads
Tap Delete advertising ID if that option appears
Confirm your choice
Depending on your Galaxy model and software configuration, you may also find Google's advertising controls through Settings > Google > All services > Ads.
Deleting the advertising ID prevents apps from accessing that particular Google advertising identifier. It does not prevent every form of advertising, analytics or device identification.
Open SettingsTap Security & PrivacyTap Privacy controlsTap AdsTap Delete advertising IDConfirm your choice
Open Settings
Tap Security & Privacy
Tap Privacy controls
Tap Ads
Tap Delete advertising ID
Confirm your choice

Google says deleting the advertising ID removes that identifier. Apps that try to access it receive a string of zeros instead. Apps can still have their own privacy and advertising settings, so this does not eliminate every form of tracking.
Next: tighten location permissions
Now look at which apps can see where you are and whether they really need that access.

Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap Location ServicesScroll through the list of appsTap an app you want to reviewChoose the appropriate access, such as Never, Ask Next Time or When I Share or While Using the AppIf the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Precise Location
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Location Services
Scroll through the list of apps
Tap an app you want to review
Choose the appropriate access, such as Never, Ask Next Time or When I Share or While Using the App
If the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Precise Location
You don't have to turn Location Services off completely. Doing so can interfere with useful features. Instead, focus on apps that have more access than they need.

Open SettingsTap LocationTap App permissions or App location permissionsReview the apps that can access your locationTap an app you want to changeSelect the appropriate option, such as Don't allow, Ask every time or Allow only while using the appIf the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Use precise location
Open Settings
Tap Location
Tap App permissions or App location permissions
Review the apps that can access your location
Tap an app you want to change
Select the appropriate option, such as Don't allow, Ask every time or Allow only while using the app
If the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Use precise location
Pay particular attention to apps allowed to access your location all the time. Weather, shopping and similar apps often don't need continuous background access.
YOUR HOME IS EMPTY. DO BURGLARS ALREADY KNOW?
Data broker listings often include sensitive details like your address, phone number and relatives, making removal a critical first step. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Open SettingsTap LocationTap App location permissionsReview the apps under categories such as Allowed all the time, Allowed only while in use, Ask every time or allow when I share and Not allowedTap an app you want to changeChoose the level of location access it actually needsTurn off Use precise location when an approximate location is enough
Open Settings
Tap Location
Tap App location permissions
Review the apps under categories such as Allowed all the time, Allowed only while in use, Ask every time or allow when I share and Not allowed
Tap an app you want to change
Choose the level of location access it actually needs
Turn off Use precise location when an approximate location is enough
A weather app, for example, usually doesn't need to know exactly where you're standing. Navigation is one situation where precise location makes much more sense.
Then: clear out what you're not using

Delete dormant apps. Every unused app is another set of permissions and data practices you may have forgotten about. If you haven't opened an app since last year and no longer need it, consider deleting it.
Finally: do it for your parents too

If you have older relatives, their phones are worth checking next. They may be carrying years of old app permissions, and scammers frequently target older adults. Sit down with them for 10 minutes the next time you visit. Review location permissions, advertising controls and apps they no longer use.
The half your phone settings can't reach

Changing these settings can reduce future collection and sharing, but it doesn't erase information that companies may have already collected. And here's the piece many people miss. A location trail by itself may consist largely of coordinates and device information. It becomes much more revealing when someone can connect those movements with a name, home address, phone number or relatives. Some of that identifying information can come from people-search and data broker sites that publish or sell personal details. You can run a quick free scan to see what a scammer would see if they looked you up right now. If it shows details you never agreed to publish, you'll be able to take action and get them removed.

This is where I strongly recommend using a personal data removal service. These services can automatically send removal requests to hundreds of data brokers, including people-search websites, on your behalf. They can also keep monitoring and resubmitting requests when your information reappears, which is important because data can return even after it has been removed. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

Your phone can reveal far more about your life than you may realize. Location data can expose visits to doctors, pharmacies, places of worship and other sensitive locations, especially when it gets combined with advertising identifiers and other information about you. The FTC's actions against location data brokers show this is not a hypothetical privacy problem. And the Gravy Analytics breach showed what can happen when enormous collections of location information fall into the wrong hands. I would start by reviewing which apps have access to your location and removing access from anything that doesn't truly need it. Then limit app tracking on your iPhone or delete your advertising ID on Android if that option is available. These changes won't make you invisible, but they can reduce the amount of information available to build a detailed trail of where you go. And don't forget the phones belonging to parents or older relatives. Years of forgotten app permissions can leave far more information exposed than they realize.
