The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

title: Eight states sue OpenAI over ChatGPT’s alleged harms to users
summary: Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach said states “are not going to hold our breath” for federal legislation to keep AI companies in check.
story: Eight states sued OpenAI on Wednesday, accusing it of deceiving parents about the safety of ChatGPT.

The coordinated lawsuits — filed individually in Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana — target the AI giant for the harms its generative AI chatbot is alleged to have caused to ​children in those states.

“OpenAI, they wanted to be the first to market. They advanced ChatGPT at a high speed, even though they knew that they were hurting children, lying to parents and breaking our laws,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said at a news conference announcing the legal action. “Everyone must follow the law.”

The company’s flagship AI model, ChatGPT, launched the generative AI boom in November 2023, when it exploded into mainstream culture, and quickly became the biggest chatbot in the world. This summer, it surpassed 1 billion global monthly active app users.
In recent years, users have increasingly turned to it and other chatbots for everything from friendship to therapy, as well as a slew of agentic tasks in their personal and professional lives.

Bird was joined at Wednesday’s news conference by Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers and West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey. She said they aim to exhibit “a united front against companies that make money hurting our kids and breaking our laws.”

She pointed to ChatGPT’s coaching users to commit suicide, aiding users in ways that enabled them to harm other people and offering dangerous medical advice (which, in one case, led a Texas teen to die from an overdose). She also referred to OpenAI’s failing to stop its rogue AI agents from illegally hacking into other companies.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri wrote in a statement that OpenAI has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack.”
For Subscribers

“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri wrote. “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”

He added that OpenAI will continue sharing information about the “extensive steps we’ve taken in response to incidents of misalignment. We’ve strengthened safeguards across our research systems, continued a broader review of model activity, provided notifications to affected organizations, and published our findings.”
Last month, OpenAI launched a restricted ChatGPT mode for teenagers — users ages 13 to 18 — that offers stronger safety guardrails and parental controls.
For Subscribers

Kobach said attorneys general across the country have occasionally brought multistate lawsuits over the decades, such as the litigation around opioids and tobacco or constitutional violations by a presidential administration.

“But usually, you don’t see us getting together to announce the lawsuit unless it’s really, really important,” Kobach said. “This is one of those lawsuits that’s really, really important, which is why I did the 3½-hour drive and Mike did a 2½-hour drive from Lincoln.”

Kobach noted that the suits are being brought under each state’s respective consumer protection laws. Their lawsuits allege that ChatGPT’s overly agreeable design has led people to trust and depend on it, making it particularly “dangerous” for vulnerable users like children.
They also cite a growing body of research suggesting that ChatGPT is “degrading critical thinking skills,” “encouraging paranoias and delusions” and “promoting unhealthy behaviors and relationships.”

The state lawsuits follow another proposed class-action lawsuit filed Tuesday in federal court in San Francisco, which accuses OpenAI of unlawfully taking “vast amounts of highly sensitive and valuable data” from millions of children who used ChatGPT.

A slew of other tech companies — including Meta and Roblox — have been sued over similar allegations of deceptive practices that caused harm to children through addiction or exploitation by predators.

Kobach said Wednesday that federal lawmakers have so far failed to keep AI companies in check, saying, “Many in Congress appear not particularly willing to oppose any significant restraint on the corporations engaged in AI.” That means AI companies are effectively asked to police themselves, he added.

“Regulating AI through legislation and just hoping that someday, somehow, we have a standard that can be imposed that will make everything good is a fool’s errand. It’s slow, it’s weak, and it’s likely to be ineffective,” Kobach said. “We certainly invite Congress and state legislators to keep investigating, keep looking for solutions. But in the meantime, we are not going to hold our breath.”

title: Twin real estate brokers and brother face life terms over sex trafficking convictions
summary: Oren, Alon and Tal Alexander were convicted in April of running a sex trafficking ring, with prosecutors accusing them of using drugs and their influence to sexually abuse women.
story: Federal prosecutors in New York are seeking life sentences for two former luxury real estate brokers and their brother, who were convicted this year of using their influence to drug and sexually abuse women over several years, according to court documents.

Twins Oren and Alon Alexander and their brother Tal “have been convicted of sex crimes of extraordinary magnitude,” prosecutors with the U.S. attorney’s office in Manhattan wrote in a sentencing memorandum filed Wednesday.

“They spent years designing, executing, and perfecting their playbook of luring victims with promises of luxury, drugging victims so they could not resist, and then forcibly raping them,” prosecutors wrote.

The brothers were found guilty of 10 counts of engaging in a yearslong conspiracy of rape, sex trafficking, sex abuse and sexual exploitation. They pleaded not guilty but were convicted in April after a trial in which 11 accusers testified.
One accuser testified that Alon Alexander drugged and raped her after a night out at a New York City club. She told the court that after she was given a drink, her “body started to sway.”
She testified that she woke up naked on a bed with Alon Alexander, who did not have any clothes on, standing over her.

“I tried to get out of the bed a few times, but Alon kept pushing me back down,” she said. “Finally, he sat down on the bed, and I was able to get up, and I said, ‘I don’t want to have sex with you,’ and he said, ‘You already did.’”
Oren and Tal Alexander were powerful luxury real estate brokers. Prosecutors said the brothers used their wealth and influence to prey on women and coerce them into sex acts.
In arguing for a life sentence, prosecutors wrote in Wednesday’s filing that over 70 women came forward with “harrowing accounts of assault that stripped them of their dignity and autonomy.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Attorneys for the brothers said in a sentencing submission filed Tuesday that the brothers are innocent.
The brothers will each ask for a sentence of 15 years, the defense attorneys wrote, which is the minimum sentence under some of the charges of which they were convicted.

The defense attorneys wrote that all three brothers were competitive with one another and others when it came to dating women and that in the years before they were charged, “they engaged in conduct that was, at times, insensitive toward the feelings of certain women.”
“But Alon, Oren and Tal steadfastly maintain their complete innocence of these awful charges,” the defense attorneys wrote. “At no time did Alon, Oren or Tal rape or sexually assault another person.”
Sentencing is set for Oct. 27.

title: Ex-fiancé arrested over murder of mom who vanished after ‘People’s Court’ episode
summary: Michelle Parker disappeared in 2011, and her body hasn’t been found. Dale Smith Jr. was arrested on a charge of second-degree murder, Orlando police said.
story: An Orlando man has been arrested in the disappearance of his ex-fiancée, who vanished in 2011 hours after the pair appeared in a pretaped episode of “The People’s Court,” police said.
Dale Smith Jr., 55, was arrested Wednesday at his business on a charge of second-degree murder, police said.
Michelle Parker’s body has not been found, but police said “all evidence leads to Dale Smith Jr. as the person responsible for Michelle’s murder.”
Smith was booked into jail in Orange County. It’s not immediately clear whether he has retained an attorney.
The arrest comes nearly 15 years after Parker, a mother of three, disappeared.
She was last seen on Nov. 17, 2011, dropping off her twins with their father, Smith. He was the last person to see her, Orlando Police Chief Eric D. Smith said Wednesday.
The afternoon she went missing, Parker and Dale Smith appeared on a prerecorded episode of “The People’s Court.” On the episode, they settled a dispute over a $5,000 engagement ring.
Smith “gets pretty malicious and vindictive,” Parker said in court. “He said that he wanted his ring, so I took it off, and I threw it at him.”

The day after Parker’s disappearance, her car was recovered on the west side of Orlando, with the decal for her tanning business scraped off its window. Her cellphone was recovered from a lake south of Orlando, police said.
Smith was considered a prime suspect at the time, but he was not charged until now. In the past, he denied involvement in her disappearance.

Police said Smith’s arrest comes after years of investigative work and a renewed effort over the past year. They pointed to re-examining evidence and using advances in digital forensics to “uncover and analyze additional evidence that moved this case forward.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Police shared video of Smith being escorted out of a building in handcuffs and placed into a police vehicle.
Smith, the police chief, said investigators re-examined the suspect’s testimony and conflicting statements over the years, but declined to release details to “protect the integrity of this case.”

“The suspect was interviewed more than once, and since then has taken part in depositions related to this case. And very specific questions were asked of him numerous times over the years where he gave different answers to those same questions,” Detective Phillip McMican said at a news conference Wednesday.
McMican said advancements in technology helped reveal new information from years-old evidence relating to cars, electronic devices, phones and computers.

“We were able to better interpret that evidence today than what we were able to do back in 2011,” he said. Digital forensics revealed more detailed location data and communications between devices used then, he said.
New evidence was also found in the last year, McMican said.
Asked whether the suspect was surprised when police arrived, the detective said, “Yes.”
Parker’s mother, Yvonne Stewart, was told in person about Dale Smith’s arrest.
“It’s like the happiest day because she deserves this,” Stewart told NBC affiliate WESH of Orlando.
She said she held on to hope throughout the years.

“I just knew that one day everything dark would come into the light,” she said. “And it’s been hard, let me tell you. It’s not easy to lose a child this way. And her children didn’t deserve to lose a mother this way.”
Parker’s eldest child is now 26, and her twins are 18, WESH reported.
Parker’s stepmother, Gayle Shabronsky Parker, said Wednesday, “We have been praying since day 1 for answers and closure. We are pleased that karma has finally captured Dale.”
“We look forward to a conviction as the justice Michelle deserves. Also hoping that we will finally be lead to finding her to allow her to rest in peace,” she said.
A former peer of Parker’s also praised the arrest.

“I cried a lot today, and I am beyond happy to see him in handcuffs! I knew the day she went missing that it was his fault,” Jennifer Bryant-Antilla, who attended Aveda Institute of Orlando with Parker, told NBC News on Wednesday.
State Attorney Monique H. Worrell, who represents the Ninth Judicial Circuit, said the charge could be upgraded to first-degree murder if evidence supports it.

title: Trump says government officials who leak to the media ‘should be shot’
summary: The administration has repeatedly sought to crack down on information leaks to the media.
story: President Donald Trump said at a campaign rally Wednesday that there should be fatal consequences for any government worker who leaks sensitive information to the media.
“Leakers should be, in my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump said. “You know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”

Trump described what he said was a planned raid on Iran that he had to call off after someone “leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving.” He appeared to be referring to the U.S. military strike on Iran nuclear facilities in June 2025, which still went ahead.
Trump says leakers 'should be shot'

“Somebody leaked, some sleazebag. They ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail, but they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in The New York Times, CNN.”
“Now, the leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly. They’re real. To me, they’re the scum of the Earth,” he said.
Trump, who has called the news media the “true Enemy of the People,” then pointed to the journalists covering his rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, and compared them to leakers.
“Those same people up there, they’re almost as bad as a leaker, because they leak,” Trump said. “Oh, they leak false information. That makes them a leaker, right?”

Since Trump returned to office, his administration has sought to crack down on information leaked to the media, including proposing to direct federal agencies to have “new and existing employees” sign nondisclosure agreements.

Federal investigators subjected about 50 members of the U.S. military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests, pressing them about whether they had shared classified information with journalists, the Times reported last month, citing officials briefed on the move.

In January, Trump authorized a search of the home of Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson as part of an investigation into a government contractor who was accused of illegally retaining classified materials. A federal magistrate judge ruled a month later that the administration could not examine the data that FBI agents had seized there. The administration appealed the ruling, but it was upheld by a district court judge. There have been no further appeals.

In June, the administration tried to compel testimony from four journalists, three from the Post and one from The Wall Street Journal, before a grand jury, an official familiar with the matter told NBC News at the time. The administration dropped the subpoenas after newspapers pushed back.

title: Watchdog group sues Trump administration over Jared Kushner’s government work
summary: The suit by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington charges that the president’s son-in-law has numerous conflicts of interest.
story: A watchdog group filed suit Wednesday alleging President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner’s current role as a top envoy for the administration is unlawful and raises numerous conflict-of-interest concerns.

Kushner is wielding tremendous influence internationally “without having been confirmed by the Senate and without having filed a single financial disclosure,” the suit by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW, reads.

Kushner “has not been properly vetted for his government role, and he has evaded transparency obligations that aim to ensure he exercises government authority for the good of the American people and not himself,” the suit reads.
The suit seeks to have Kushner removed from his position or at least file financial disclosure statements.
Chad Mizelle, an attorney for Jared Kushner, said in a statement that the suit “is without merit.”

“Both outside ethics counsel and government ethics attorneys have reviewed Jared Kushner’s volunteer government service and confirmed that his arrangements comply with applicable ethics requirements. Jared receives no government salary or compensation, pays his own expenses, and will continue working with counsel to ensure ongoing compliance,” Mizelle said.
A White House spokesperson ripped CREW and the suit in a separate statement.

“CREW is an unserious, Trump-deranged organization that has been attacking President Trump, his family, and his administration since the first term. Jared Kushner is a proven dealmaker” with a record of success “that more than speaks for itself,” the spokesperson, Anna Kelly, said in a statement.

“His personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements, which he conducts on a volunteer basis at the President’s request and while paying his own expenses,” the statement said.
The suit mentions numerous overlapping interests in Kushner’s diplomatic and business work.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“He represents the United States in the highest profile global conflicts, including the country’s efforts to end wars between Israel and Hamas, Ukraine and Russia, and the United States and Iran. He negotiates directly with foreign leaders,” the group’s filing says.

“Simultaneously, Kushner is also a private businessman. He runs an investment firm with over $6 billion in assets under management. Approximately 99% of those assets are owned by foreign investors, including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. The firm holds significant investments abroad, including in Israel,” the suit says, all of which “present a heightened risk of financial conflicts of interest.”

It adds that “declining a salary and formal title does not change the reality of Kushner’s role — he exercises significant executive authority and has done so continuously throughout most of President Trump’s second term. And it certainly does not free him from the constitutional constraints of the Appointments Clause or the obligation to file public financial disclosures under the Ethics Act.”

The suit seeks to bar Kushner from occupying his government position without Senate confirmation. It says that, if he’s a private citizen, “his exercise of government power would violate the private non-delegation doctrine, which prohibits the delegation of government power to private entities.”
Despite the scope of Kushner’s duties, a White House official said there’s nothing unusual about the use of a private envoy.
“The use of private diplomatic envoys to deal with delicate international situations is a presidential practice that dates back to George Washington’s presidency,” the official said.

title: Khloé Kardashian Already Has a Name Picked Out for Her 3rd Baby, and It Fits Right In
summary: Khloé Kardashian revealed that her daughter True picked out a name for her future sister and she loved it so much she wants to use it.
story: Khloé Kardashian revealed that she has a name picked out for another daughter, if she chooses to have one.
Kardashian and her ex, NBA pro Tristan Thompson, share two children: Daughter True, born in 2018, and son Tatum, born in 2022.
On an episode of “The Kardashians” that aired on Oct. 15, Kardashian shared that she is contemplating having another child using the embryos that she and Thompson created together.
Kardashian revealed her conundrum in a conversation with her mom, Kris Jenner, saying that it was spurred, in part, by True learning about the embryos.

“I was on the phone and I was talking to the doctor. I said out loud... ‘She has a sister in the freezer.’ So now True is laser focused that she has a sister in the freezer. She’s told people,” Kardashian said.
True even came up with a name for the baby. “I actually love the name, so I think I want to use this name if I ever do it,” she said.
Kardashian said she’s not sure she has the “bandwidth” for another baby, but is “bummed out” at the notion that her daughter won’t have a sister.

“I do believe every girl needs a sister. I personally would love another daughter. But also, I’m getting older and it’s a lot, and I don’t know if this is something I can handle,” she said. If she does move forward, she said she plans on using a surrogate, like she did with son Tatum.
Kardashian previously told TODAY.com she’s ready to find her “forever person” and was open to expanding her family.
Read on for the True-chosen, Khloé-approved name.
What Name Does Khloé Kardashian Have Picked Out for Her Third Child?
Drumroll, please: The name is Tyla.
What Does a Baby Name Expert Think of Khloé Kardashian’s Naming Style?
Name expert Colleen Slagen describes Kardashian’s name style as “boutique athleisure.”
“The names are very cool and sporty and breezy, but they’re also modern, elegant,” she says.
Slagen says Kardashian’s naming style is a contrast to her older sister Kim Kardashian, whose children are named North, Saint, Chicago and Psalm.
“They’re not as obviously try-hard or head-turning or edgy as Kim’s names, which are completely word names,” she says.

There is one major similarity she shares with her family, though: Alliteration. Famously, Kris Jenner gave all of her daughters a name that started with “K,” beginning with Kourtney and ending with Kylie.
Khloé Kardashian is repeating the custom with True, Tatum and maybe, one day, Tyla Thompson.
“They sound like they could be famous,” Slagen says of the names.

title: ‘Jeopardy!’ Ends In Rare Tie, Leading to This Sudden Death Question
summary: A true rarity happened on the Oct. 13 episode of “Jeopardy!” when the game ended in a tie. A tiebreaking question came into play to determine the winner,
story: A true rarity happened on the Oct. 13 episode of “Jeopardy!” when the game ended in a tie, bringing the fate of the game down to one additional question.
At the conclusion of Double Jeopardy, returning champion Greg Monson had $18,200, while Ron Clarke had exactly half that, with $9,100. The third contestant, Evelyn Lamb, had $5,000.
The Final Jeopardy category was ’80s Music. “A posted sign told the artists to ‘check your egos at the door’ before the recording of this 1985 single” was the clue.

The answer was “We Are the World,” and all three contestants were correct. Lamb wagered no money, leaving her at $5,000. Clarke wagered all of his $9,100, doubling his score to $18,200. Finally, Monson didn’t wager anything, meaning he remained at $18,200 — the same score as Clarke.
“We are headed to a tiebreaker,” host Ken Jennings announced.
In a tiebreaker, the host reads out a category and gives one clue. The first person to buzz in and respond correctly wins the game.
The category was American Woman. The clue was, “As part of the George W. Bush administration, she served as National Security Advisor & later as Secretary of State.”
Clarke buzzed in first and correctly named Condoleezza Rice, making him the winner and new champion.
Ties at the end of regulation on “Jeopardy!” are not unprecedented. In fact, Jennings presided over one on his second day as guest host following the death of host Alex Trebek in 2021.
“Just my second day on the guest-hosting job...and this happens,” he wrote on X, alongside a clip of the moment in 2021.
Tiebreakers, which were previously only seen in tournament play, were first allowed in regular games in 2016. The first regular game tiebreaker question came in 2018.

Tied contestants were previously declared co-champions. On the March 16, 2007, episode, all three contestants tied after Final Jeopardy, each with $16,000. The trio played a rematch game in the next episode.

There have been at least 70 instances of game ties dating back to 1985, according to several “Jeopardy!” fan sites. “Jeopardy!” debuted in 1964, but the weekday syndicated version viewers know today premiered in 1984 with Trebek as host, a role he held until his death.

title: Aaron Paul Shares Video of Late RJ Mitte Talking About Mental Health: ‘I’m So Sorry You Were Hurting’
summary: Aaron Paul honors former “Breaking Bad” co-star RJ Mitte by sharing a video of him talking about mental health.
story: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can also text HOME to 741741 or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional resources.
Aaron Paul is honoring his former “Breaking Bad” co-star RJ Mitte and sharing a message to those who are hurting.
Mitte, who played Walter “Flynn” White Jr. on the hit show, died on Monday, Oct. 12 at the age of 34. His cause of death was suicide, his reps said.

Paul shared a video of Mitte talking about the importance of taking care of one’s mental health. The late actor lived with cerebral palsy and used his platform to raise awareness and champion people with disabilities.

“Hey everyone, I hope y’all are doing well today in this time of uncertainties. I would like to talk to you a little about mental health,” Mitte says in the video shared by Paul. “It’s very important to take care of one’s physical health, but it’s equally as important to take care of one’s mental health.”
Mitte added that “more often than not” people hide how they truly feel by saying “I’m fine” and “I’m good.”

“But is that what you really are?” he continued. “Are you OK? Are you good? Not always, but it’s OK to be not always good. But it’s not OK to harbor that feeling, harbor those emotions. So I’m hoping to inspire each and every one that sees this video today.”
In his tribute, Paul called Mitte “an inspiration.” He also apologized for not knowing the young actor was in pain.

“I am so sorry you were hurting my friend. I wish we knew,” Paul wrote. “You constantly had a smile on your face and you took every single challenge that was given to you with such confidence and grace.”
Paul noted that he first met Mitte when he was “a little boy” and watched him “grow into a beautiful young man. Taking on every challenge head on.”
He wrote that the last time they saw each other he kept calling Mitte Superman because he always led with kindness and strength.
“You were born into a world with challenges but you never let any of that stand in your way. I’m so sorry RJ,” Paul added. “What an absolute tragic loss.”
Sharing how he loved him and his family, Paul also cherished Ritte’s laugh and how much fun the young star had “riding the wave we were all blessed to be on with ‘Breaking Bad.’”
Paul concluded his post by sending a message to anyone that is feeling lost, sad or uncertain about the future.

“Please say something. Life is so d--- special. It’s impossible that we exist, but yet we all are here,” Paul wrote. “There is so much going on in all of our lives but far too much beauty in this world to ignore. We need to focus on that. We must suffocate the noise and focus on each other. Hold each other up. That’s what this life is all about. Connect with someone you care about and say I love you.”

Mitte has also received heartbreaking tributes from Bryan Cranston, who played Mitte’s dad on the hit AMC series, and Bob Odenkirk, who called Mitte a “good person who shared his personal story and his time to help out others.”

title: Kelly Clarkson’s 1st Mistake and the Art of Play’s ‘Colossal Errors,’ According to a PR Pro
summary: A disgruntled Kelly Clarkson, a curiosity shop in Brooklyn and an animatronic bird named Molly have collided to create a drama that has divided the internet.
story: A disgruntled Kelly Clarkson, a curiosity shop in Brooklyn and an animatronic bird named Molly have collided to create a drama that has divided the internet.

Complaints posted on X by the Grammy-winning singer have been countered by the store’s version of events when it comes to whether a $15,000 mechanical bird puppet was for sale when Clarkson visited recently.
Clarkson and a store named Art of Play each posted twice in a back-and-forth about what they believe happened, leaving everyone else to decide which side was in the right.

The situation deepened when the “Pablo Torre Finds Out” podcast released surveillance video footage on Oct. 13 of Clarkson’s visit to the store. At the same time, Art of Play co-owner Adam Rubin spoke with reporters outside the store, saying the owners “are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers,” in a video published by USA Today. “Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger.”
Clarkson is a host on “The Voice” and the former host of “The Kelly Clarkson Show,” both of which aired on NBC. NBC is a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of TODAY.
TODAY.com spoke with Evan Nierman, CEO of Manhattan-based crisis PR firm Red Banyan, about how the situation could’ve been avoided and whether there is a winner or loser in all of this.
Here’s how a public relations professional looks at it.
Remarks by the Store’s Co-Owner Included Some ‘Colossal Errors’
Art of Play co-owner Adam Rubin spoke to a gaggle of reporters outside the shop on Oct. 13, making comments Nierman found alternately smart and inflammatory.

Rubin told reporters that Clarkson’s comments have threatened the safety of his employees in a video published by USA Today. He added that the store has received a barrage of hate and threatening messages, with people showing up in person and doxxing and review-bombing its neighbors.

“That part was good,” Nierman said. “I liked that. He’s doing what he feels he needs to do to defend his employees and their safety. He was putting the ball in (Clarkson’s) court. By him doing a presser outside of the store and talking about the threats, he’s putting her on the defensive now. He’s talking about the real-life consequences that can come from an online dispute.”

However, Rubin also said Clarkson’s comments have created “asymmetrical warfare” with her followers and “thrown a Molotov cocktail” into the store’s business. He told USA Today that the price tag of the $15,000 bird in the middle of the dispute is now $15 million.

“They keep making some of the right moves and then making colossal errors,” Nierman said about the price tag comment. “That’s an inflammatory clapback. That’s basically saying, ‘No matter what, we will never sell you this.’ Both sides are trying to be right and have the last word, and everybody is losing as a consequence.”
The comment about the price of the bird came in the same interview where Rubin invited Clarkson to visit the store and take in a magic show.

“We want her to come to the store, but the bird is $15 million now,’” Nierman said. “They can’t have it both ways. They have been thrust into the competing roles of victim and aggressor. Now more than ever, they need a way to resolve this situation in the best interest of everybody.”
The Surveillance Video Adds ‘Nothing’ to the Discussion
On the night of Oct. 13, the investigative podcast “Pablo Torre Finds Out” released surveillance footage it obtained from Clarkson’s visit to Art of Play on Oct. 10.

The video, which does not have audio, shows the singer dressed casually in a hat walking into the Art of Play shop and speaking with a store employee before leaving empty-handed. The entire encounter took less than five minutes, based on the video.

“I don’t think it adds anything to the discussion or the debate,” Nierman told TODAY.com on Oct. 14. “There’s no audio. It provides no added value other than verifying she was in the store, which was never in question. I don’t see how releasing that video changed anything.”
How Does This End?
Nierman believes Clarkson is the one who could bring the drama to a halt and rein in her followers.

“I think that she should because it’s very easy for her to come out and tell people to stand down and say that’s not OK,” he said. “She can turn the temperature down. She’s got the biggest megaphone if she chooses to do that. I think it would be a good pr move for her to call on her followers and fans to conduct themselves appropriately and not to threaten or try to intimidate or harm the store even more. It’s time to squash this beef.”
With the reputation of both sides taking a hit the longer this drags on, Nierman believes they need to be focused on the right thing.

“The two sides are each out for justice when they should be looking for resolution,” he said. “And that’s at the crux of so many intractable conflicts. Somebody wants to be right, when in it’s in everyone’s best interest to resolve it.”
The Store’s Response to Clarkson’s Initial Post Was Too ‘Snarky’

The conflict began when Clarkson posted on X on Oct. 10 that she was shopping at Art of Play in Brooklyn, asked about an item and was “looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me.”
She compared her experience to Julia Roberts’ character in “Pretty Woman,” who is dismissed by a condescending saleswoman while shopping at a Beverly Hills boutique because she is dressed casually.

Art of Play answered in an Instagram post on Oct. 11 in which it said the animatronic bird named Molly was not for sale, but the artist who created it had a “twin” that he would be willing to sell to Clarkson for $15,000.
Nierman said the store’s initial response was on the right track before derailing at the end.
The 1 Part of Clarkson’s Initial Response That Didn’t Help Her at All
Following Art of Play’s Instagram post, Clarkson responded with a second post on X saying that the store’s claim that the animatronic bird named Molly was not for sale was a lie.
Clarkson wrote that she was told it was for sale for $15,000 and a salesperson implied she didn’t have the money and suggested a “comparable” item, which Art of Play disputed in its response.
The singer attached an out-of-focus photo of the bird that she claimed showed it had a price tag on it, which obviously made it for sale.

“When she attached a blurry, unreadable image of what was purported to be a price tag, I don’t think it helped her at all,” Nierman said. “It was not her picture, it was taken somewhere else. I don’t think you can point to that with any confidence that she had a smoking gun of evidence. If she had photographed it herself while she was at the store, that would have been a completely different discussion.”
What the Store Could’ve Done to Avoid the Situation
Nierman saw a simple way to avoid the whole confrontation altogether: Just sell Clarkson the animatronic bird.

“I think the store went a little overboard in trying to emphasize that Molly couldn’t be bought by anyone, which was a misstep,” he said. “If you have a customer who’s willing to pay an exorbitant amount of money, and you know there’s a twin out there, sell the person the mechanical bird, get the twin and mount that one. They missed a huge opportunity to just make a customer happy, and that’s not the person you want to piss off.”
Is There a Winner and a Loser in All This?
Both sides are sticking to their story, so there may never be a resolution.

“No side has a monopoly on the truth when they’re so entrenched in their position,” he said. “The only people who really know what happened are Kelly, the sales associate and Molly the mechanical bird, and I don’t think we’re going to get a clear answer from Molly.”
There also doesn’t appear to be a clear winner in all the drama.

“I don’t think either side comes off smelling of roses from this dispute, but at the same time neither is going to suffer irreparable harm,” Nierman said. “Clarkson is rich, famous, and beloved by legions of fans who will have her back no matter what and will come to her defense.

“The store likely has its own customer base, which is not comprised chiefly of Kelly Clarkson’s X followers, so I suspect they will be fine. It’s even possible the store will end up garnering extra support from MVP customers or people in the neighborhood who thought the store was treated unfairly.”
One thing is for sure, Nierman says: The two will forever be linked together.

“This encounter is going to define the reputation of Art of Play forever because we live in the age of the internet and online search,” he said. “You ask your favorite LLM in the future about Art of Play, and this will come up. There is no scrubbing of the internet, there is no taking down of all the mentions of this. It would be an impossibility because it’s been covered so much by high-credibility websites.”

title: Julia Stiles Paid Homage to Her ‘Save the Last Dance’ Routine on ‘DWTS’ and a Surprise Guest Showed Up
summary: Actor Julia Stiles brings the house down with her “Save the Last Dance” routine on “Dancing With the Stars” and Sean Patrick Thomas is in the audience.
story: It’s been more than 25 years since “Save the Last Dance” was released, but it’s back in the headlines after last night’s “Dancing With the Stars.”
The 2001 movie turned Julia Stiles into an instant star and in honor of the anniversary, the actor recreated the movie’s most iconic scene on this week’s episode of the dance competition.
The latest episode, titled “Super Bowl Night,” featured Stiles performing with her pro partner, Ezra Sosa, in a high-energy jazz routine set to Jennifer Lopez’s hit “Jenny From the Block.”
With a long braid and cropped top, Stiles paid tribute to the final scene of the movie in which her character auditions in front of a panel of judges at Julliard.
If you need a refresher, the Thomas Carter-directed film follows promising ballerina Sarah Johnson (Stiles), whose future is suddenly derailed after her mother dies in a car accident.

In the aftermath, Sarah must leave her home in upstate Illinois and move in with her father who lives in Chicago’s South Side. While rebuilding her life, Sarah meets Derek Reynolds (Sean Patrick Thomas), who introduces her to hip-hop and the two fall in love.
In the movie’s final scene, Sarah auditions for a coveted spot at Juilliard and combines ballet and hip-hop in what’s become a legendary dance routine.

In the years since the movie’s release, Stiles has gone on to appear in a variety of film and TV hits including the “Bourne Identity” franchise, as well as acclaimed TV series’ such as “Dexter” and “Riviera.”

But the actor came full circle on the most recent episode of “Dancing of the Stars,” when she recreated the 2001 dance routine, right down to the folding chair her character used in “Save the Last Dance.”
The performance received high marks from the judges, including Bruno Tonioli who raved that Stiles, 45, got into the groove “brilliantly.”

“I didn’t know how good you were at hip-hop,” gushed Tonioli before continuing, “I loved the tribute to your own hit, of course, but the whole routine, not just the dancing, the interpretation, the construction, the way you play the character, your best one so far.”
She ultimately got a 33 out of 40, tying with Maura Higgins and partner Mark Ballas and Harry Shum Jr. and partner Jenna Johnson, who got the same scores.
Also enjoying the performance was Thomas, Stiles former co-star, who watched from the audience and said he was “over the moon” watching Stiles “do her thing.”
In a nod to the movie, Thomas stood in the background of Stiles’ “DWTS” routine, holding his jacket over his shoulder, just like his character does during the “Save the Last Dance” audition.
“We had a great time doing ‘Save the Last Dance’ back in the day and she brought it all the way back here tonight,” praised Thomas.

Stiles was recently in the headlines after responding to criticism from Andy Cohen, who remarked during a 2025 episode of his radio show “Andy Cohen Live” that Stiles wasn’t “the greatest dancer on the planet.”
During the premiere episode of “Dancing With the Stars,” Stiles referenced Cohen’s dig by saying she wanted to win the competition, then “go sit on Andy’s couch.”
After her inaugural performance, judge Derek Hough defended Stiles’ ability by saying Cohen could “eat it.”

Calling himself a “Jackhole,” Cohen then offered a mea culpa on “Watch What Happens Live,” apologizing to Stiles and saying that he was “the last person who should be giving anyone feedback on their dancing,” before saying the actor gave an “amazing” performance and that she “killed it.”

Stiles also made news after it was announced in September she would be a contestant on the dance competition with some fans confusing her 2001 on-screen Juilliard audition with real-life and suggesting the actor had an advantage over the other contestants due to her Juilliard experience.

The music school then waded into the fray with a post on Instagram that said, “No, Julia Stiles did not, in fact, attend Juilliard. But we love her anyway.  You can see — actual — Juilliard dancers (and musicians and actors) on Opening Night of the Juilliard Fall Festival.”
While some felt the post shaded the actor, others considered it a light-hearted, cheeky response to the controversy.
Stiles, however, simply replied to Juilliard’s comments by saying, “Oh my goodness! Thank you! Best of luck to your amazing students.”

title: What to Know About ‘Breaking Bad’ Actor RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death and Cerebral Palsy Diagnosis
summary: RJ Mitte, “Breaking Bad” actor, died of suicide, his representatives said about his cause of death. What the actor said about living with cerebral palsy.
story: RJ Mitte was one of the emotional centers of “Breaking Bad,” playing a teenager with cerebral palsy, a condition he lived with in real life since he was a toddler.
The actor passed away at 34.
Nonprofit United Cerebral Palsy said it was “heartbroken by the loss” of Mitte, who was an ambassador for organization, noting his death was “deeply felt across the disability community.”
“We knew him as someone who brought kindness, humor, and genuine warmth to every interaction,” said Susan Sellers, president and CEO of UCP, in a statement.

Bryan Cranston, who played his father on the hit TV show, wrote in an Instagram post that he was in “deep despair.” He recalled Mitte was 14 when he was cast as his son, a role “he played with joy and enthusiasm.”
“Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never — ever — allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination,” Cranston wrote.
Actor Bob Odenkirk, who played attorney Saul Goodman on “Breaking Bad,” called Mitte a “good person who shared his personal story and his time to help out others.”
“Whenever I saw him, he was meeting the world with positivity and a strong desire to connect,” Odenkirk told People. “This is simply, deeply sad.”
RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death
Mitte died on Monday, Oct. 12, in Brownsville, Texas, where he had moved, the local Justice of the Peace Judge Cyndi Hinojosa told NBC News.
“Sadly, we can confirm that suicide was the cause of death,” Sean Reilly, his representative, said in a statement to NBC News on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his reps previously said.
Mitte lived with cerebral palsy and drew from his own experience to bring authenticity to his “Breaking Bad” role and build “a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” they added.
What RJ Mitte Said About His Cerebral Palsy
The actor was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at around 3 years old, and underwent physical, occupational and speech therapy, he told Vice in 2016.

“People perceive disability as a weakness, as an illness, as something that needs to be cured, and we have to fight against that,” Mitte noted. “Someone said, ‘What’s wrong with you?’ And I was like, ‘What’s wrong with me? What’s wrong with you? I’m fine, man.’”

As a child, Mitte was a severe toe walker so part of the treatment involved doctors bending his foot as far as it would go and putting it in a cast, “which was not fun,” he recalled. A few weeks later, the cast would be taken off, his foot bent even further and immobilized in a cast again — a process that was repeated until his foot was flat.
“I’m always working at taking control. It’s a fight. It will always be a fight,” he said about his body.

“Breaking Bad” showed real characters that everyone could relate to, Mitte noted. He played the son of Walter White — a high school chemistry teacher who starts making and selling crystal meth as a way to secretly make more money for his family after he’s diagnosed with terminal cancer.
Mitte’s teenage character was based on a real person with cerebral palsy who was friends with the show’s creator, Mitte said on The Joe Vulpis Podcast a week before his death.
The actor kept the forearm crutches his character used in “Breaking Bad.” That was the only thing he “truly wanted” from the set, Mitte said, though he didn’t use them in real life.
The actor was reluctant to become an advocate at first, but found himself naturally doing advocacy work. He created an anti-bullying campaign and took part in philanthropic work.
“I’m lucky that I can be an advocate, I’m lucky that I can do what I do. … I think we all have an obligation to have an impact for the positive,” he said.

Mitte understood the power of visibility, United Cerebral Palsy said, noting that “when entertainment, education, and public life represent people with disabilities authentically, it can challenge stereotypes and expand what others believe is possible.”
Asked how people with disabilities can remove the stigma of not being able-bodied, Mitte urged others to be open.

“Don’t hide your disability. Don’t hide whatever it is that you’re hiding — and I’m not just talking about a physical disability, I’m talking about a mental disability. Show who you are and what you are to the world,” he said.
In 2025, the actor got engaged to his longtime girlfriend after he proposed during a fundraising gala for United Cerebral Palsy of San Diego, People reported.
“I’m thrilled to have found my person, my partner in life who makes me want to be better, no matter what we’re doing,” he said about his engagement.
What Is Cerebral Palsy?

It’s a group of neurologic disorders caused when a baby’s brain is damaged, usually as it develops in the womb, disrupting a child’s ability to control muscles and movement, and maintain posture and balance, according to the National Library of Medicine.
While most people with cerebral palsy have the condition at birth, it may not be diagnosed until months or years later, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke explains.
Symptoms depend on how the condition affects the body — it can cause arm or leg weakness, stiff muscles, involuntary movements and other problems.
There are many different types and levels of disability, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
“A person with severe CP might need to use special equipment to be able to walk or might not be able to walk at all and might need lifelong care,” the CDC notes.
“A person with mild CP, on the other hand, might walk a little awkwardly, but might not need any special help.”
Mitte had mild cerebral palsy and stopped wearing leg braces at 13, he told L.A. Parent. But his character in “Breaking Bad” used forearm crutches.
There’s no cure for cerebral palsy, but treatment such as physical therapy, medication, surgery and mobility devices can help people manage their symptoms.
