The singer then continued with her version of events.

“So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.’” she wrote in the post, appearing to convey sarcasm. “That all never happened and now it’s not for sale.”
The singer also hit back at criticisms that she doesn’t support small businesses.

“You don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business,” she wrote. “It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception.”
She concluded by saying, “Your store is really cool.”
“Unfortunately, you aren’t,” she wrote.

Art of Play did not immediately respond to TODAY.com’s request for comment on Clarkson’s Oct. 11 post. The store, however, shared a follow-up post to its Instagram early Oct. 12 in an effort to “clarify one additional detail about Kelly Clarkson’s visit.”

“During the 5 minutes she spent in the store, she inquired about our mechanical bird puppet named Molly,” the Oct. 12 post from Art of Play said. “We explained that while Molly is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a de facto mascot for our shop, a nearly identical automaton is owned by the creator of the machines, a brilliant artist named Bliss Kolb who lives in Seattle. He told us he would be willing to part with Molly’s twin for $15,000.”
The store said employees offered to show her another option for a singing bird that was available to take home that day for $2,000 but Clarkson “did not stick around long enough to see it.”
Art of Play said it reached out to the singer directly to “clear the air.”
Art of Play, which sits in the neighborhood of Brooklyn Heights, is a specialty store that features home goods in addition to magic-themed gifts, cards and games.

In her post, Clarkson said that she “drove all the way to Brooklyn” to take a peek at the store, already with a few things in mind to purchase. She compared her experience to that of Julia Roberts’ “Pretty Woman” character Vivian Ward when she is brushed off by a Beverly Hills salesperson who assumes she can’t afford the expensive items in the store because of her casual appearance.
Art of Play said in the statement that the store invites all shoppers to play with their items.
“And they do, many stay for hours enjoying our puzzles, games and toys,” the store said.
The criticisms they’ve been receiving have taken them by surprise, the store said in the statement.

“Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store,” the statement said. “It’s been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity.”

The bird automaton appears to have not been available for purchase in the past. Several weeks ago, the store had made a post about their “favorite items not for sale,” featuring an image of the bird automaton.

Since the parties’ comments, the internet has been divided with Clarkson’s fans flocking to the store’s pages to express their disappointment. Many others, including New York locals, have been commenting as well, sharing their positive experiences with the shop.

title: Ashley Padilla is a Mom Trying To Hold it Together After Babysitter Canceled on ‘SNL’
summary: Ashley Padilla joined the Weekend Update segment of “Saturday Night Live” as a frazzled mom whose babysitter canceled.
story: It’s hard to keep it together when you’ve had it up to here!

Ashley Padilla joined the Weekend Update segment of “Saturday Night Live” as a frazzled mom whose babysitter canceled. Given the circumstances, problem child Coco, played by new cast member Grace Reiter, had to tag along as well.
While the mom tried really, really hard to provide the desk with some cute fall ideas for the family, Coco seemed to have other plans.
“She’s my little buddy tonight because someone just wasn’t getting along with the sitter,” the mom explains during the Oct. 10 episode.
Coco adds with a sinister look in her eyes that she “broke another one.”
In the sketch, the frazzled mom attempts to share some sweet activities like pressing a leaf into a book — one of her “favorites.”
“Mommy picks a book, and Coco goes and fetches a beautiful orange and red leaf from the yard,” the mom says.
Coco, however, shares how the activity really went down.
“I fell into a pile of leaves, and no one knew where I was for a day,” Coco says.

While the pair bicker, things really unravel when Coco claims she was missing for so long, she didn’t have dinner. According to Coco, the pizza her mom says she ate doesn’t count because she “didn’t like it.”
And mom just loses it.
“It doesn’t matter if you don’t like it,” the mom says, shrieking. “It’s still dinner if you ate it. You ate it all, and that’s dinner because you ate it.”
The mom attempts to share another lovely activity — making dried apple dolls.
“And fun fact: We got the apples just this weekend at a beautiful local apple orchard,” the mom says.
Coco, of course, has something to add.
“My mom stuck me in the corn maze for three hours so she could kiss a farmer,” she says.
Let’s just hope that the mom finally finds a worthy babysitter for Coco. She deserves a break.

title: Ben Affleck Reveals Hilarious Reason Why Matt Damon Passed Up Lead Role in ‘Animals’
summary: Ben Affleck reveals why his best friend, Matt Damon, couldn’t take on the leading role in his new Netflix thriller “Animals” as he had once hoped.
story: Ben Affleck reveals why his best friend, Matt Damon, couldn’t take on the leading role in his new Netflix thriller “Animals” as he had once hoped.

Affleck, who directed and starred in the new movie joined the Oct. 11 episode of Sunday Sitdown to chat about the film. And he revealed that Damon, initially his top pick to star in flick, had some other plans instead.
“I’m sure you’re aware, Ben, you were not the director’s first choice to star in this movie,” host Willie Geist joked.
Affleck confirmed the detail, explaining that Damon got another professional opportunity.

“Matt then ended up getting offered this little, kinda s----- little movie, ‘The Odyssey’ that bombed. And he was very embarrassed by it, of course.” Affleck said, laughing. “It just didn’t work at the box office, or with the critics, which happens sometimes.”
The “Animals” star went on to praise his friend, he played titular character Odysseus.
“He was really as happy as I’ve ever seen him the day that he got that job,” Affleck told Willie of Damon.
Damon and Affleck have been well-known besties, going through their first massive Hollywood moment together as they won the best screenplay Oscar in 1998 for “Good Will Hunting.”
“The whole idea of even being there was absurd,” Affleck recalled to Willie of attending the Oscars. “The year before, we’d watched the show from an apartment in Somerville, Massachusetts.”
The two have since acted in multiple films together including “The Last Duel” in 2021 and “Air” in 2023.

Additionally, Affleck has launched multiple production companies with Damon including Artists Equity, founded in November 2022. The company is behind a number of titles including “Air” and new film “Animals.”

The crime thriller, released Oct. 9, follows a high-profile Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped, forcing the hopeful and his wife, played by Kerry Washington, into coming up with the $7 million ransom amid a financially stressful time in his campaign.
“I make movies mindful of the audience. But also, I did some things I really wanted to do in this that I think were really interesting,” the actor and director said of the new film.
Affleck beamed over his newest project, “I love this movie, ‘Animals.’ I really want people to see it.”

title: Mike Ditka’s Perfectly Unhinged Version of ‘Take Me Out To The Ballgame’ Resurfaces After Death
summary: A resurfaced video of Chicago Bears icon Mike Ditka singing during the seventh inning stretch at a baseball game is giving many fans something to smile about as they grieve the football giant’s death.
story: A resurfaced video of Chicago Bears icon Mike Ditka singing during the seventh inning stretch at a baseball game is giving many fans something to smile about as they grieve the football giant’s death.
The video features Ditka singing the classic “Take Me Out To The Ballgame” during a July 1998 match at Chicago’s Wrigley Field. And he definitely puts his own twist on the song.

In the clip, shared by MLB, Ditka raucously belts out the words, losing his voice several times throughout the song. Adding to his undeniable aura, Ditka also speeds up, leading the organist to attempt to match his pace.
It’s controlled chaos — just like the beloved football icon himself.
Ditka’s family announced his death Oct. 9. He was 86.

The Bears icon, who led the team to its only Super Bowl victory in  1986, was known for his big personality as much as he was for his gridiron prowess. And that charisma certainly shined during that 1998 Chicago Cubs game against the Pittsburgh Pirates.

That wasn’t even Ditka’s only famous rendition of the ballpark song. During a 2005 game at Wrigley Field between the Cubs and the Philadelphia Phillies, Ditka was joined by comedian Will Ferrell to lead the stadium in the song. The pair, who starred in comedy “Kicking & Screaming,” don’t exactly sing in-sync.

Ditka, who was inducted into the pro football Hall of Fame in 1988, has long been a source of comedy fodder. He even became the focus of a recurring sketch on “Saturday Night Live” in which a group of superfans, who look just like Ditka himself, hail the legendary coach as something of a god.

title: Alexander Skarsgard’s See-Through Dress Shoes Are Causing Chaos Across The Internet
summary: Actor Alexander Skarsgard showed up in a pair of see-through shoes to the annual BFI London Film Festival for an Oct. 8 screening of his upcoming romantic fantasy movie “Wicker.”
story: To call this a bold fashion choice would be an understatement.

Actor Alexander Skarsgard showed up to the annual BFI London Film Festival for an Oct. 8 screening of his upcoming romantic fantasy movie “Wicker.” But his look quickly became a focus of the event as he rocked a pair of see-through oxford shoes on the red carpet.
The shoes unsurprisingly elicited a range of responses from disgust to extreme lust.
Skarsgard’s transparent black shoes, which featured vinyl laces, were paired with a gold, metallic suit.
The oxfords, from fashion house Saint Laurent’s spring 2027 collection, made waves earlier this year when they debuted on the runway at  men’s Paris fashion week in June.

Corrado De Biase, the brand’s freelance design director of shoes, explained that the look is called “O. Fan,” after adult online platform OnlyFans. The shoes, he told Women’s Wear Daily, are a celebration of sexuality in the gay community.

“Because Monsieur Saint Laurent himself was really linked to those young community people when he was young,” De Biase told the outlet. “So it’s normal that a brand like us looks at that kind of thing. It’s been part of the house from the beginning.”
Saint Laurent creative director Anthony Vaccarello had a snarkier explanation for the footwear.
“I asked myself: ‘Why torture women with plastic shoes, but not men?’” Vaccarello said, according to WWD.
People across the internet had their own interpretations of the look. Some couldn’t help but wonder how Skarsgard was faring in the no-doubt sweaty shoes.
Others were just thirsting over the fashion choice.
“Oo our steak is too juicy, our lobster is too buttery, Alexander Skarsgaard is showing too much foot,” one commenter wrote on Instagram.

Well, 2026 appears to be the year of the gutsy red carpet footwear. Margaret Qualley sported a pair of Chanel’s “shoeless shoes” to the world premiere of “The Dog Stars” in August. The shoes were essentially black heels that were strapped to Qualley’s feet with two sets of laces and no soles.
While some deemed the shoes as chic, others joked that the barely-there footwear was a sign of “shrinkflation.”

title: Ben Affleck Admits He Trash Talks Kids Online While Playing ‘Fortnite’
summary: Ben Affleck recently revealed on the “New Heights” podcast that he sometimes gets into squabbles with kids on the internet while playing popular multiplayer open-world survival game “Fortnight.”
story: Gamer rage gets to everyone — even celebs.
Ben Affleck recently revealed on the “New Heights” podcast that he sometimes trash talks kids on the internet while playing popular multiplayer open-world survival game “Fortnight.”
Affleck, it appears, has a tough time taking the heat.

“Twelve-year-olds just f--- you up,” Affleck lamented to hosts Travis Kelce and Jason Kelce on the Oct. 7 podcast episode. “I get killed right away and they taunt you and s--- like ‘You suck! F--- you!’”
Affleck acknowledged that he ends up “getting in arguments” with the kids in the game’s chat.
“F--- you! I don’t suck,” he says in response to the taunting, Affleck told the podcast hosts. “I’m a grown man.”

Affleck, who’s currently promoting crime-thriller film “Animals,” joined the podcast to discuss the project. He explained that the costumes in the film are inspired by some of the outfits, referred to as skins, in “Fortnite.” The video game famously features different skins that can be upgraded through milestones, challenges and more.
As Affleck points out in the podcast, the game has also dropped exclusive and limited edition skins that have become some of the most coveted aspects of the game.
“My son and he’s like ‘For Christmas, can you get me these real skins for Fortnite?’ But they’re 300 bucks,” Affleck tells the podcast of the virtual costumes.
Affleck has long been an avid gamer. On the podcast, he explained that in addition to first-person shooter games, he’s a fan of sports games like football game “Madden” and basketball game “NBA 2K.”

The actor has also been open about his love for “Valorant,” a first-person tactical hero shooter video game. He’s been spotted at major tournaments and even joined a watch party livestream last year with esports team Sentinels.

title: ‘We’re done’: Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries as anger at Trump mounts
summary: Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the United States of betraying Kyiv with a “dangerous” withdrawal of support critical to its defense against Russia.
story: Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the United States of betraying Kyiv with a “dangerous” withdrawal of support critical to its defense against Russia.

Ukraine held off on attacks for three days after President Donald Trump’s unilateral “energy ceasefire” announcement, but accused Russia of repeatedly attacking its power grid. Zelenskyy voiced mounting frustration over the Kremlin’s failure to abide by the truce, and what he sees as U.S. attempts to pressure Kyiv after gaps in intelligence sharing on Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink internet service.

Satellite internet functionality via Starshield — the military version of the SpaceX service — was being at least partially restored Thursday, according to a source in the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the topic.
In an interview with the Financial Times, published Thursday, Zelenskyy indicated his patience had already been exhausted.
“The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying.

Hours later, a fire was reported at an oil refinery in the western Ryazan region, Gov. Pavel Malkov said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”

Ukraine has been reeling from a sudden shift from Trump, who struck a diesel deal with Russia in an apparent bid to relieve pressure at the pump ahead of the midterm elections. He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil facilities and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader.
Trump’s “energy ceasefire” appeared to take both warring sides by surprise. He has blamed the Ukrainian campaign for fueling a rise in energy prices, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.
The moves caused frustration and confusion in Ukraine and Europe, intensifying concerns over how much of an ally the U.S. remained in the fight against Russia.

That worry was exacerbated Wednesday when Kyiv said it was facing the slowing down of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite  terminals, disrupting battlefield missions and its ability to intercept Russian drones attacking Ukrainian cities.

Ukraine was swarmed by Russian drones Wednesday and, since early Thursday, more than 850 had filled the skies over Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. “And this comes precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted,” he said, referring to the Starlink slowdown.

Musk, a staunch ally of Trump, wrote on social media that decisions on restricting the use of Starshield, the military version of his company’s satellite system, were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.
Overnight, Musk said it was “time for Zelenskyy to go.”

The Defense Ministry source said Kyiv was still seeking clarification on the reasons for Wednesday’s throttling of the technology, on which Ukraine relies for battlefield communication, drone operations and air defense.

It came amid mounting questions about whether the U.S. has stopped or limited the sharing of critical military intelligence with Ukraine, after Zelenskyy said several ballistic strikes on Kyiv did not come with the usual advance warning from its partners.

Coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves were likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

Ukraine was concerned that the chain of events amounted to an effort to pile pressure on Kyiv and backtrack on years of U.S. promises to help fend off the Russian invasion, one of the Ukrainian officials said.

Ukraine relies heavily on U.S. intelligence and the Starshield satellite network to defend itself against Russian drone and missile attacks and to target Russian forces with its own drones. A reduction in intelligence assistance or satellite access could seriously undermine Ukraine’s battlefield prospects just as winter sets in, according to military experts.

Ukrainian military officials were told by their U.S. counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence,” Zelenskyy said, according to the Financial Times, although it was subsequently presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch.

The withdrawal of the intelligence and simultaneous weakening of Starlink satellite internet were “dangerous” for Ukraine at a time when Russia is intensifying its strikes, he told the newspaper, adding that fighting without the U.S. would be “very difficult.”
In a separate interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy acknowledged he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s actions.
The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on Zelenskyy’s accusations and the renewed Ukrainian strikes.

title: Britain faces ‘new era’ of security threats from Iran and Russia, MI5 says
summary: Britain’s MI5 boss Ken McCallum warned of a range of threats posed by Russia, Iran, China, AI and terrorist groups.
story: LONDON — Iran is escalating its campaign of threats on British soil, expanding attacks beyond dissidents abroad and Jewish sites to now focusing on harder military targets, the country’s domestic intelligence chief said Tuesday.

MI5 Director General Ken McCallum was speaking less than two weeks after the United States rushed to withdraw its bombers from a key air base in England, with American officials saying there had been reports of a possible Iranian drone attack.

Giving a wide-ranging “annual threat update” at MI5’s Thames House headquarters in London, McCallum warned that Britain and Europe had “entered a new era of national security,” which he likened to the shift that came after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

His speech comes at a moment of tumult not just for the Middle East and Ukraine, which continue to be ravaged by war, but also the rest of Europe, which has suffered so-called hybrid aggression from Moscow and Tehran including sabotage, arson and cyberattacks. European governments are now openly telling people to stockpile food and prepare for more of their taxes to be spent on defense, warning that Russia may launch a direct attack on their soil.
MI5 is now devoting more resources than it had during the Cold War to countering threats from countries such as Russia, Iran, China and others, McCallum said.
“Russia remains aggressor No. 1, as Putin’s Kremlin continues to lash out at the U.K. and its allies,” he added.

But another arch belligerent is Iran, whose leaders have been “attempting to expand their hybrid campaign” of “using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations and Israeli sites,” the spy chief said.

“Much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities, with whom I want to express solidarity,” he said. But this year has seen a shift of “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.”
Over the past year, intelligence operations have led to more than 50 Iran-linked arrests in Britain, he said.

McCallum made reference to the incident last month at RAF Fairford, the military base in rural England from where the U.S. had been launching bombers involved in the assault against Iran. He declined to give details, citing ongoing investigations and operations, but said the case was “not unique.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Details are hazy, but in the early hours of Sept. 27, a member of the public called the police after spotting three vans in a country lane near the base. Seven men in their 20s, one of them a dual British-Iranian national, have been arrested and released on bail. Authorities said they found only gasoline in the vehicles.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in Parliament on Monday that the incident “is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed” by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the powerful political, military and economic group that holds huge sway in the country.
A week after the incident, Washington hastily withdrew its bombers from the base because, according to two U.S. officials, of reports of a possible drone attack against the site.

On Tuesday, McCallum downplayed fears that Iran could mount such a complex attack, saying it has so far been hiring unsophisticated criminals for operations in the United Kingdom. But he warned that could change.

On Russia, McCallum said its military and intelligence services “are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare,” being careful not to trigger NATO’s Article 5 threshold, in which other countries would be expected to defend their allies.
“We see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding,” he said. “The whole aim of hybrid tactics is to try to intimidate us.”

Within the U.K.’s “multifaceted relationship with China” — Beijing is a major trading partner to London — MI5 has been focused on efforts by the Chinese government “to conduct espionage, coercion or democratic interference.”
On Al Qaeda and the Islamic State terrorist group, or ISIS, MI5 still has to respond “to attempts to carry out mass casualty attacks,” he said.
But perhaps the gravest warning came when it came to artificial intelligence, which he said in the future could be used by terrorist groups and other actors to create new “bioweapons.”
And “beyond misuse of AI by human adversaries sit the potential risks posed by AI itself,” he said.

“Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are. Is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel. And deserves the serious attention it is getting, including in MI5.”

title: Energy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine
summary: Oil and gas prices rose Monday after an “energy ceasefire” announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday failed to gain traction.
story: Oil and gas prices rose Monday after an “energy ceasefire” announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday failed to gain traction.
Brent crude oil jumped 2% to almost $108 per barrel and U.S. crude oil rose more than 2% to about $94. Meanwhile, diesel futures fully erased a small drop they saw last week.

Just weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the price pressures are mounting. Republicans face a steep climb to maintain their majorities in Congress, and voters across the country cite high gas prices as a key issue affecting their votes.
The average nationwide price of diesel fuel Monday was $6.26 per gallon, nearly 80% higher than it had been at the start of the year, according to AAA data.
The rising prices Monday came less than 24 hours after Trump declared that a ceasefire had been agreed to.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Shortly after the president’s post, Russia renewed strikes against Ukrainian energy assets.

Pressed by reporters Monday as to why neither the Kremlin nor Kyiv had firmly committed to his ceasefire, Trump indicated that he knew when he made the announcement on Sunday that he did not yet have a commitment from either side.

“They agreed, you know why? Because I said ‘You agree,” Trump told reporters at the White House. As for getting Russian President Vladimir Putin to commit, Trump said, “We’re going to see what happens.”
Asked if he was aware that Russia had already violated the ceasefire Trump had announced, the president replied, “I’m not sure about that,” before claiming there had been “violations on both sides.”
Ceasefire déjà vu

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine learned about Trump’s ceasefire from media reports and was given no advance warning. He reiterated his position that Ukraine was open to an agreement not to target enemy energy infrastructure as long as Moscow agrees to it, too.
In the meantime, Russia continued with “glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that a power plant in Kharkiv had recently been attacked.
“Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet,’” Zelenskyy said, using the Russian word for “no.”
The Kremlin on Monday neither confirmed nor denied having agreed to a deal.
Trump’s Sunday announcement closely mirrored a similar post he made in September, when he announced that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”

There, too, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s participation hinged on Russia’s agreement to comply, which never came. Neither Ukrainian nor Russian strikes on the other’s energy assets slowed down in September.
Trump’s deal with Putin

The dubious ceasefire Trump declared over the weekend followed a stunning announcement Friday in which the president said Russia would supply millions of barrels of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.”
The announcement came after a phone call Friday between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin that reportedly lasted over an hour.
For Subscribers

Trump said the deal with Putin would “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” That would translate into about 2.25 million barrels of diesel, or less diesel than the United States uses in just one day.
For Subscribers
Further details and logistics of Russia’s plan had yet to be announced Monday.
In addition to the Russia deal, Trump has pressured G7 allies to release more diesel fuel supplies in recent days and lifted domestic restrictions on an off-road variety of diesel.
In order to clear a legal path for the diesel deal, the Treasury Department announced a six-month suspension of the fuel sanctions imposed on the Kremlin in 2022 for its illegal invasion of Ukraine.
Ukrainian officials, European allies and some U.S. lawmakers were aghast at the deal and the U.S. decision to unilaterally ease Russia sanctions.
Trump defended the deal Monday, calling it “the right choice for the American People.”
Trump also said more diesel fuel would be made available “within a short period of time,” if Russia’s refineries could produce it.
Questions about Russia’s capacity
Yet experts are highly skeptical that there will be any significant resumption of Russian diesel exports in the near term.
Due to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia, refiners that produce oil, gas and diesel have suffered heavy damage.

“Reported gasoline output is down by 20% compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%, prompting the government to restrict fuel exports to protect domestic supplies,” analysts at the International Energy Agency wrote in a September report.
For weeks, Trump has focused on the price of diesel fuel, which began rising as a result of the Iran war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
In July, escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war began adding to the pressure on diesel prices.
As Ukrainian drones systematically targeted Russian energy assets, the Kremlin responded by restricting diesel exports in order to preserve its supply for domestic use.
Until then, Russia had been one of the world’s top exporters of refined oil products, which include diesel fuel.
Russia said Friday that it would lift some of its export restrictions in order to accommodate the deal with Trump. But it was unclear how fast that would happen.

title: Harry and Meghan cheered on first joint appearance since returning to U.K.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, were making their first royal-style public appearance together Thursday since they returned to the United Kingdom with their two children.
story: LONDON — Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, were making their first royal-style public appearance together Thursday since they returned to the United Kingdom with their two children.
Harry, 42, and Meghan, 45, were visiting three charities in Nottingham, as they look to rebuild their image in Britain six years after walking away from royal life.

Nottingham, a city in central England known as the setting for the famous “Robin Hood” legend, holds a special place in the couple’s history as the place where they made their first joint public appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017.
“It’s almost a full circle moment because it looks very much like a royal engagement,” NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash said.

title: Pope Leo slept well after cancer surgery, but recovery could take ‘longer than expected’
summary: Peru’s president said the 71-year-old American pontiff’s planned visit might be in jeopardy as he recovers from surgery to remove part of his right lung.
story: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV’s recovery from lung surgery could take “longer than expected,” the president of Peru warned Wednesday, as the leader of the Roman Catholic Church continued to mend at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital.
Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru, which was set to start Nov. 11.

“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said. “We will also be watching for any announcements from the Vatican, because we understand that his recovery will take several weeks longer than expected and, therefore, we also understand that there could be some changes to the schedule of his visit.”
Leo, who is a Chicago native, spent more than two decades working in Peru and maintains close ties with that South American country.

Fujimori’s announcement was somewhat at odds with the Vatican’s assertion on Wednesday that the pope was recovering as expected after an operation to remove part of his right lung, which confirmed a cancer diagnosis.

The medical team taking care of the 71-year-old said he had undergone routine blood tests and a chest X-ray and that, so far, the results “confirm a normal post-operative course: the values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed.”
The pope has begun walking around his hospital room and ate both breakfast and lunch on Wednesday, they said.
So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.

In the meantime, the Vatican released its first post-surgery message from the pope, which was addressed to the participants at a meeting to mark the 10th anniversary of “Amoris Laetitia,” a 2016 document on Catholic doctrine released by Pope Francis.

“As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days,” the message stated. “I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church.”
As the pontiff continues with recovery, his brother, Louis Prevost, is being treated for blood cancer, a source close to the Prevost family told NBC Chicago.
In an interview with Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty, Prevost said they’re optimistic the pope will rally.
“They caught it early enough, and he’ll be able to heal from the surgery and go on with his papal ministry,” he said.
Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.
Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.

Leo spent a calm night in the hospital after surgery to remove a malignant lung nodule was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned,” the Vatican said Tuesday. Leo was in the operating room for nearly three hours, it said.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.
The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.

Following his surgery, the pontiff “woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor,” the Vatican said. The room is next to the usual papal apartment, complete with private chapel, which is currently undergoing renovations.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.
The cancer diagnosis could complicate his busy schedule.
Just weeks earlier, hundreds of thousands of people packed the streets of Paris for an outdoor Mass on a visit that saw Leo warn about the risks of artificial intelligence.
He was planning to take a historic two-week visit to South America next month, although it is unclear if that will still go ahead.
Messages of support and sympathy flowed in after the news.
Dr. Fernando Daniels III, a 67-year-old physician from Maryland, was among many praying for Leo’s swift recovery in the Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square.
“I’ve seen miracles in medicine. I’ve seen people told with terminal illnesses they wouldn’t live and they did,” he told NBC News.
“Prayers of all should heal him,” said Daniels, who was traveling as part of a group.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife, Jeanette Rubio, were praying for the pope.
“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X.
“We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation,” New York City’s Archbishop Ronald Hicks said in a statement.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, the German Catholic news agency KNA reported.

“The pope’s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” Steinmeier was quoted as saying.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Vatican City, Mithil Aggarwal from Hong Kong and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.

title: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of restricting Starlink, disrupting military amid Trump pressure
summary: Ukrainian officials and military units accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling a technology at the heart of their battlefield communications and drone operations.
story: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of undermining its ability to defend itself by limiting Starlink internet services as it reeled from intense Russian ballistic missile attacks that it said came without the usual warning from allies.

Musk put the responsibility for the restrictions on President Donald Trump’s shoulders on social media, saying the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is owned and controlled by the U.S. government.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said.
A spokesperson for President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NBC News that the limitations remained in place late Wednesday.

Facing pressure from Trump to halt strikes on Russia’s energy industry, Kyiv and its backers have worried that Washington could cut off battlefield support to try to force it into concessions at the negotiating table.

Ukrainian officials and their European partners were already scrambling to understand the status of U.S. intelligence-sharing after the lack of alert ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv this week, two Ukrainian and two European officials told NBC News.

Trump insisted the U.S. was still sharing intelligence, but with relations spiraling, Ukrainian officials and military units accused SpaceX on Wednesday of throttling a technology essential to their battlefield communications and drone operations.
It was not immediately clear what might be behind the Starlink interruptions, though some Ukrainian officials said the timing could not be a coincidence given that Musk is a close Trump ally.

title: What to know about Pope Leo’s lung surgery
summary: The Vatican said the procedure was done “successfully” and that the 71-year-old Leo had returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital.
story: Pope Leo XIV had surgery Tuesday to remove a lung nodule. The Vatican said that the procedure was completed “successfully” and that Leo, 71, had returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital.
Further information will be released later, the Vatican said.
Leo had the surgery after a “small, localized nodule” was found in his lung during recent routine medical tests.

A lung nodule is a small mass of tissue detected through X-ray or CT scan screening. Most nodules are benign. According to the American Cancer Society, nodules can be caused by a number of factors, including irritants such as air pollution and diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and cancer. They can also be caused by scar tissue from previous infections.
Leo said Sunday the nodule was detected “at a very early stage.”

There are several approaches to surgery, depending on the size and location of the nodule and whether doctors suspect cancer, said Dr. Ankit Bharat, the chief of thoracic surgery at Northwestern Medicine.
“When doctors decide to proceed directly to surgery rather than first obtaining a biopsy, it can suggest a higher level of concern on the lung scan,” Bharat said.

The Vatican hasn’t said yet what surgeons found during the procedure. But Leo could experience changes in his breathing, depending on how much lung tissue was removed. If surgeons needed to remove an entire lobe, his lung capacity could decrease by as much as 25%, Bharat said. Smaller procedures, such as a wedge or a segmental resection, would be likely to have a much smaller impact on his long-term lung function.
What to know about Pope Leo’s surgery to remove a lung nodule

Lung cancer is more treatable if it is caught early. The deadly cancer is most often caused by cigarette smoking, but about 20% of lung cancer cases are diagnosed in people who have never smoked or used tobacco, according to the American Cancer Society.
However, finding a nodule on a scan doesn’t confirm a cancer diagnosis, Bharat said, and the surgery will reveal more information as doctors are able to put the nodule under a microscope.
Advances in the procedures mean they are generally less invasive, and some patients begin walking within a day or two.
If the nodule is larger and more lung tissue is removed, meaning the surgery is more extensive, it may be three to four weeks before a patient is fully recovered.
“Given the pope’s age, his recovery could be slower than that of a younger, otherwise healthy patient,” Bharat said.

Leo has a major trip scheduled to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s possible he could make the trip, doctors suggest, if the surgery was minimally invasive and there are no surprise findings. If the nodule is cancerous, doctors will determine whether he can be treated while traveling or the trip may need to be postponed.

title: Why advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia
summary: Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.
story: Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.

But in recent days it has appeared helpless in the face of barrages of missiles and drones fired by the Houthi rebel group from neighboring Yemen. The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors and work from home.

The Iran-backed Houthis, once seen as little more than a ragtag militia, have grown into a formidable fighting force. They have inflicted damage on the region’s top oil producer, threatened critical supply routes in the Red Sea and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defenses failed to stop the Houthis’ attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict:
Vast arsenal

Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12% of all U.S. arms exports from 2021 to 2025.

Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defense systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers.
Saudi Arabia’s annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles.
Huge area to defend
The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia’s large size.

Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country’s sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles through rugged desert areas.

“Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday.
At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help.
Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support.
President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision.
Battle-tested

Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting.
The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defenses.

The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year.

title: Deadly Saudi airport strikes mark major Mideast escalation
summary: An attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis over the weekend appeared to be the deadliest on the kingdom in more than a decade.
story: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Fears of intensifying conflict were growing in Saudi Arabia on Monday after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched multiple strikes on Riyadh’s airport over the weekend, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds.
“What is clear is we remain on a strong escalation ladder,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a Washington-based think tank, who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region.

More than 300 people were injured when the kingdom’s main international airport was attacked Saturday, marking a major escalation in the Houthi rebel group’s campaign against the world’s leading oil exporter and key U.S. ally in the region.

Among the victims were one American, as well as four citizens of Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshi nationals, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Palestinian, a Syrian and one Sudanese national. The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia later said that an Indian national injured in Saturday’s attack had died.
Video capturing the Saturday attack showed a packed airport before the flash of an explosion sent people running for safety as debris falls on them.
The airport remained shut Monday.
The impact of the attacks was felt at the WPC Energy Congress in the Saudi capital Monday, with several top energy executives dropping off the event’s schedule.

The chief executives of Exxon Mobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which started Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organizers released early Monday, Reuters reported. The energy giants did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NBC News.

“You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said, according to Reuters, as he opened Monday’s session of the gathering held just miles away from Riyadh airport. But, he added, “our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”
He said the stepped-up fighting was serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious.”
“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix,” he separately said. “We come out of the ashes all the time and every time.”

Fighting on the ground in neighboring Yemen is also intensifying, with the Houthis expanding their operations along its Red Sea coast and around the Bab el Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 after the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

A period of relative calm following a 2022 ceasefire was shattered in July when the Houthis resumed attacks after accusing Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was attempting to land.

Baron said the latest attacks — the deadliest by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade — could have a “galvanizing effect” on Washington and other international actors, including Pakistan and Turkey, which recently reached a joint defense agreement with the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia defiant following multiple strikes on Riyadh

“As these attacks are growing stronger and stronger, on the one hand, it’s increasing the hurt on the kingdom, but it’s also increasing assessments for many that there has to be some strong effort to degrade the Houthis and restore deterrence,” Baron said.
Washington faces mounting pressure. President Donald Trump on Saturday said he was still weighing whether to join in Saudi Arabia’s military operations against the Houthis.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it,” he told reporters. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

After sweeping gains by Houthi forces in Yemen last month, Trump said the rebel group had contacted the U.S. to stress that it doesn’t “want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”
While the skies over Riyadh were empty Monday after flights in and out of the capital were canceled, roads were full of traffic as residents tried to get back to normal life.
And in the early hours of Sunday, road crossings at the border with the United Arab Emirates were largely deserted.

“With the Houthis, we knew that they could hit Riyadh airport, but it’s almost about the precision,” Baron said. “There’s a great degree of anxiety in terms of ... living in a world where you can just have random armed groups hitting airports.”

title: Pope Leo to be hospitalized Tuesday for surgery to remove a lung nodule
summary: The 71-year-old revealed the discovery during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors’ advice to remove the nodule “in the coming days.”
story: Pope Leo XIV will be admitted to a hospital Tuesday morning to undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule discovered during recent medical tests, the Vatican said Monday.
The timing of the procedure was confirmed after the 71-year-old American pontiff had a full day of meetings, audiences and appointments.
The Vatican press office also said no particular issue precipitated the tests, denying Italian media reports suggesting an inflammation had prompted the medical checkup.
Leo revealed the discovery during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors’ advice to remove the nodule “in the coming days.” The Vatican predicted a weeklong recovery.

It was business as usual at the Vatican on Monday, with Leo presiding over six private audiences, including with the head of the U.S. military chaplains, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, and one group audience. He also made three appointments, and the Vatican released a letter he had penned to the outgoing dean of the College of Cardinals.
In the afternoon, he was expected to rejoin a weeklong conference he convened on ministering to families.

Leo’s surgery marks the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. It was significant because the pope himself revealed the news, in perhaps the most public way possible: at the end of his Sunday noon blessing, with thousands of people in St. Peter’s Square.
For Subscribers

The Vatican has for centuries zealously guarded the pope’s health and has often sent out confusing information, or none at all, about papal illnesses. Pope Francis tried to change that by being upfront about his frailties and musing on his eventual death. But even during his pontificate, information was tightly controlled.
For Subscribers
Leo’s decision and reveal suggested an unusual level of transparency by the American pope.

A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended to ascertain whether it is cancerous since performing a lung biopsy by needle can be difficult.
Oncologists say that if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.

title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire, but Kyiv says strikes continue
summary: President Donald Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, only for the two sides to continue their aerial attacks on each other’s energy facilities.
story: President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict. There was no confirmation from Moscow, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he heard the news through the media.
Ukrainian officials said Russia continued to attack its energy facilities. Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, only for the two sides to also continue their aerial attacks then.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” He did not elaborate further on what the ceasefire might include.
Zelenskyy said Monday that Ukraine “didn’t know about it. We learned from the media.”
He told the Warsaw Security Forum that “we do support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side, and this looks strange.”
Ukrainian officials said Russia carried out further strikes in the hours after Trump’s announcement and on Monday morning, including against an energy facility on the outskirts of Kharkiv.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Trump’s announcement of a ceasefire that “contacts are ongoing. When we have anything to say on this topic, we’ll be sure to keep you informed.”

It follows a dramatic few days in which Trump agreed to a diesel deal with the Kremlin, demanded Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. The shift left Kyiv and its European allies reeling.

The U.S. agreed Friday to lift sanctions on Russian fuel in a deal that Trump said would see Russia “immediately” release 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and global marketplace,” followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.

title: Saudi airport struck again a day after deadly attack
summary: The Saudi-led coalition said a projectile struck a terminal at Riyadh’s airport Sunday, a day after a missile attack killed 13 people and injured 309.
story: An unidentified projectile struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport Sunday, injuring people a day after a deadly missile attack at the same site raised questions about whether the United States would join another conflict in the region.

Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation confirmed the death of a Pakistani resident and injuries to 11 others in the new attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. It said authorities were assessing damage and checking the safety of airport facilities.
The Saudi-led coalition said the projectile struck Terminal 4, causing a fire that authorities were working to control. It also reported intercepting and destroying a cruise missile near the airport.

Saturday’s strike killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The victims included one American as well as four citizens of Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshi nationals, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Palestinian, a Syrian and one Sudanese.
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Sunday that an Indian national injured in Saturday’s attack had died. The embassy said it was in contact with the family and would help repatriate the remains.
Some of the wounded were in critical condition, authorities said, while airport operations remained suspended Sunday.
President Donald Trump said afterward that the U.S. was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it,” Trump told reporters. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Saturday’s strike drew widespread condemnation and intensified pressure on the kingdom and its allies to respond to the Houthi rebels. The attack was the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade and marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen-based Houthis’ campaign against the leading oil exporter, which has already rattled the global economy.

Saudi Arabia’s government and its allies blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s strike. The group did not immediately claim responsibility for the latest attack, although it renewed a warning to stay away from Saudi airports.
Washington also blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s assault, the latest of several on the busy facility in the past week. Three people were killed there in an attack on Thursday.

The attack has drawn fresh scrutiny of Washington’s response to the widening conflict, in which the Houthis have hit Saudi energy infrastructure and seized territory that gives them leverage over shipping in the Red Sea.
Trump responds to potential U.S. involvement after Saudi attack
The U.S. launched a three-month bombing campaign against the Houthis last year to stop them from targeting shipping through the critical waterway, an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudis will be looking to allies like Pakistan, Turkey, Syria, Egypt and the U.S. for help, said Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics.
“But I doubt very much whether there is an answer or even a military solution to the Yemeni conflict,” he told NBC News.

“The Houthis are determined to fight to the end,” Gerges said. “I suspect that the reason why the U.S. has been reluctant is not only because of the Iran war, but also because the U.S. tried for several months to force the Houthis to stand down, and they did not succeed.”

At the same time, the Houthis are becoming “more nimble, more resourceful, more deadly by the day, and I think what we have seen in the past few weeks is that the targeting system of the Houthis has become much more effective,” he said.

Egypt said Sunday that it “stands firmly” with Saudi Arabia, expressing “strong condemnation” for the attacks. Qatar called the missile strike “a grave violation of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security.”
Germany and Canada also condemned the attacks, with Prime Minister Mark Carney describing them as “abhorrent.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres blamed the Houthis, calling the attack “a violation of international law.” The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis called the attack a “fully-fledged war crime” and vowed a strong response.

The renewed fighting has developed alongside the broader war involving Iran, with the Houthis stepping up attacks on Saudi territory as Saudi-backed forces battle the group inside Yemen. The latest violence follows the collapse of a truce in July and a renewed Saudi-backed offensive against Houthi positions.
Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport kill 3 Saudi nationals

The Houthis have expanded their operations along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the Bab el Mandeb Strait, a critical shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Disruption there threatens international trade and energy shipments, raising fuel prices and adding another source of instability to global markets.

Trump has focused intensely on energy prices ahead of the midterm elections, including a diesel deal with the Kremlin that stunned Ukraine. But he has so far resisted deeper involvement in the Middle East.
After sweeping gains by Houthi forces last month, Trump said the group had contacted the U.S. to stress that they “don’t want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged Trump in September to take military action against the Houthis, a person familiar with the matter told NBC News.
“There is a whole lot that America can deliver,” said Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, a retired professor of political science from the United Arab Emirates.

“It doesn’t have to be in the form of going all out against the Houthis, but American sharing of intelligence, America providing the best of defense systems against Houthis’ drones and missiles is needed, and I think if that is delivered, Saudi Arabia and the rest can defend themselves,” he said.

Abdulla also called on Turkey and Pakistan to come to Saudi Arabia’s defense. The three nations signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca in August, a pact of Sunni Muslim U.S. allies alarmed at growing regional conflict.
“Now it’s the time to activate what this alliance treaty involves,” added Abdulla. “That an attack on one is an attack against all.”

title: Pope Leo says he will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung
summary: The American pope, 71, said Sunday recent medical checks led to the detection of the early-stage nodule. The procedure will take place this week, the Vatican said.
story: Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he will undergo surgery to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.
The Vatican said the procedure was planned for this week.
“Recently, during some medical tests, doctors discovered a localized nodule in my lung,” the American pontiff, 71, said during his noon prayer at St. Peter’s Square.

“It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized,” Leo said from the window of the Apostolic Palace. “The doctors believe it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed.”
The pontiff said that surgery had already been scheduled “for the coming days” and thanked onlookers for their support.
“I entrust myself to your prayers,” he said.
The news drew applause from the thousands gathered in the square before he wished the crowd a “happy Sunday.”
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement that “the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week.”
Leo announced the surgery at the end of his regular address, in which he appealed for an end to the war in Ukraine and the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea.
“The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war,” he said.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active, including weekly games of tennis.
The pontiff has a major trip scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished Leo well.
“I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days,” she said in a statement.
“The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it [today] ... are reassuring,” Meloni added.
Born Robert Francis Prevost, he became the first American pope when he was appointed in 2025.
Originally from the South Side of Chicago, he spent much of his career ministering in Peru and leading the Vatican’s powerful office of bishops.

Leo’s father, Louis Prevost, served in the Navy during World War II and worked as a superintendent of schools in the south suburbs of Chicago. His mother, Mildred Martinez Prevost, was a librarian with a master’s degree in education and two sisters who were nuns.
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died of a stroke in April 2025 at age 88 after a long hospitalization following a number of health issues.

title: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
summary: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook the central coast of Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for several neighboring countries.
story: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook the central coast of Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for several neighboring countries.

The earthquake hit around 1:56 p.m. ET, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Around three hours later, a second powerful earthquake measuring at 6.6 magnitude, struck Panama after a series of aftershocks, which registered magnitudes between 4.8 and 5.8, rippled across the southern tip of the country.
Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt.
The U.S. Tsunami Center flagged tsunami warnings for Ecuador, Colombia, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Mexico, El Salvador, Costa Rica and Peru, as well as Panama, shortly after the quake.
The initial earthquake was centered about 6 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama’s southern tip, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 6 miles.
Tremors were also felt in the capital, Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. The city is known for its tall skyscrapers.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.

“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re OK, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.”
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.

Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square and the Dos Continentes hotel.

No fatalities were immediately reported, but Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of Panama Civil Protection said injured people “have been transferred to educational centers, health centers, and hospital centers.”

The province of Coclé said the governor’s palace there suffered significant structural damage, but that staff members were safely evacuated. The local government also urged community members to remain calm in the quake’s aftermath.
Video aired by local news outlets showed a Catholic cathedral collapsing and part of a hotel’s facade falling onto a car in the city of Penonomé, in the central province of Coclé.
Social media videos show collapsed buildings near the site of the original quake and the aftershocks, including a hotel reduced to rubble in the tourist-friendly Playa Venao.
Panama’s National System for Civil Protection said it is monitoring for further reports of damage throughout the country.
Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.

Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.”
“Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he wrote on X.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.

title: State Department IG probing Kimberly Guilfoyle amid alleged $100,000 demand
summary: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and the embassy she leads are under investigation by the State Department’s Office of the Inspector General, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News.
story: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and the embassy she leads are under investigation by the State Department’s Office of the Inspector General, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News.

The government watchdog’s probe comes as legal consultant and longtime Donald Trump supporter and donor Eric Deters has accused Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her outstanding $100,000 American Express bill in the days before her 2025 confirmation hearing in exchange for access to senior administration officials.
“She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo,” Deters told NBC News in an interview Thursday.

“She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big,” he said of Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, Trump campaign surrogate and ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr.

Deters provided NBC News with a PDF document of texts and Signal messages with Guilfoyle, which were first reported Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal. The Daily Mail first reported the watchdog investigation.

One of the messages provided by Deters appears to show Guilfoyle instructing him to wire the money directly to American Express because “it won’t show up anywhere” that way. He said he did not pay her the money.
An attorney for Guilfoyle did not respond to a request for comment, but told the Journal she disputed the authenticity of the messages while not providing specifics.
Vice President JD Vance said Friday that “these are accusations” and “we don’t try people in the court of public opinion.”
Deters’ claims, he said, are “one person’s story.”
“Let’s actually see what the facts are. Let’s see what the truth is, and obviously if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it,” he said.
The White House had no comment.

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio last week asking for more information about additional allegations that appeared in The Wall Street Journal.
On Thursday, Rubio chided a reporter for asking him about the accusations against Guilfoyle while he was with her in Athens.
For Subscribers

“We don’t conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story or somebody else wrote a story because some source gave it to you,” he said, adding: “I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true.”
For Subscribers

A senior diplomatic official, meanwhile, said the news of probe set off alarm bells throughout the State Department. The official described the investigation as rare and said that watchdog is known primarily for performing routine embassy inspections rather than investigations.
A spokesperson for the State Department inspector general’s office said the watchdog does not confirm, deny or comment on investigations.
The State Department declined to comment on the accusations against Guilfoyle or any investigation.
Watchdog investigations into potential ethics violations by U.S. ambassadors are rare, but not unprecedented.

During the first Trump administration, Woody Johnson, then the U.S. ambassador to the U.K. and a longtime Republican donor,  was investigated by the State Department’s inspector general, who found he made “inappropriate” comments on race, gender and religion to embassy staff.

The State Department rejected recommendations for Johnson, saying he had watched a government video on workplace harassment and instructed senior officials to do the same, and also encouraged staff to take a training course on “mitigating unconscious bias.”

Under President Joe Biden in 2024, the watchdog investigated U.S. Ambassador to Singapore Jonathan Kaplan, finding the political appointee threatened his staff and failed to submit about $48,000 in travel expenses on time or with proper documentation.
In Kaplan’s case, State said it was taking the recommendations seriously and made organizational changes.

“The president always wants his representatives ... to manage people with dignity and respect,” former White House National Security Council spokesman John Kirby said at the time. “He’s comfortable that the State Department is taking this seriously.”

title: Navi Pillay, who led U.N. panel that found Israel committed genocide in Gaza, wins Nobel Peace Prize
summary: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay
story: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to the South African legal pioneer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for defending international law and institutions in a world in which increasingly “might overtakes right.”

Pillay, 85, has a decadeslong career that spans defending Nelson Mandela and standing up against the racist apartheid regime in South Africa, to leading a United Nations commission that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
“Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
Frydnes contrasted Pillay’s work with the wider international “shift towards power politics,” in which “international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack.”

Her “distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law,” he said. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

Pillay learned of her prize at the Nuremberg Forum, an international law gathering in Germany. She told an applauding crowd, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” prompting laughter.

That was a reference to President Donald Trump’s long-standing ambitions to win the Nobel Peace Prize, and the offer by last year’s winner, Maria Corina Machado, to share it with him as she sought support for her efforts in Venezuela.
“Everybody asks me: ‘When are you going to stop? When are you going to stop?’” Pillay said, adding that despite turning 85 last month, she had no intention of doing so.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza, namely what’s happening there is genocide,” she said.

“One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage,” she added. “But why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law and you look at all the facts.”

In later more formal remarks accepting the prize, she dedicated the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes,” warning against efforts “which attempt to weaken international criminal justice” which “risk returning us to a world in which power, rather than law, determines whose suffering matters.”

Among her many positions, Pillay previously served as a judge on the  International Criminal Court, a frequent focus of ire for the Trump administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced fresh sanctions on the body on Friday, hours after the prize was announced.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” Rubio said in a statement, threatening to continue a campaign “to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick.”
Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, was with Pillay in Germany and among the first people to congratulate her on the prize.

“This could not be a better choice at a time of attacks against international justice,” Callamard told NBC News. “She is a former ICC judge at a time when the U.S. administration is seeking to destroy the ICC,” she said, praising her work leading the U.N. commission “which found that Israel committed the crime of genocide at a time when many states are trying to defend and protect Israel’s actions.”

The ICC condemned the new U.S. sanctions Friday, and separately praised Pillay’s win as “an important recognition of the vital role that international justice plays as a cornerstone of lasting peace.”

Pillay was not among those speculated to be front-runners, who included Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of anti-Kremlin figure Alexei Navalny, Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate, and Mykola Kuleba, who founded an organization to rescue Ukrainian children abducted and forcibly taken to Russia.

The Norwegian Nobel Institute said it had has registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize, with politicians, international judges and professors among those who can put names forward. The committee that decides the winner is composed of five members appointed by the Norwegian Parliament.
The leaders of Israel, Pakistan and Cambodia all said they nominated Trump for the prize, though he said this week he didn’t think he would win.
“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Wednesday. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”

Trump did not congratulate Pillay on Friday. Instead, on Truth Social, he reposted a message from another user that said the Nobel committee had “shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned the once great Nobel Peace Prize,” describing Pillay as “an unabashed hater of America and Israel.”

title: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to discuss ‘new’ peace plan with Ukrainian delegation, sources say
summary: Ukrainian negotiators heading to the United States for a new round of talks to end the war with Russia will discuss a comprehensive new plan to help break the ongoing impasse in the conflict, a senior administration official told NBC News.
story: Ukrainian negotiators heading to the United States for a new round of talks to end the war with Russia will discuss a comprehensive new plan to help break the ongoing impasse in the conflict, a senior administration official told NBC News.

The talks starting Friday and led by special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner are the latest attempt to negotiate a settlement amid intensifying deadly aerial attacks on both sides of the border.
The discussions will center on “a new, unified proposal that is focused on all aspects of the conflict to try to end the war,” the senior administration official said Thursday evening.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian delegation will travel to the U.S. for two days of negotiations, and include Rustem Umerov, the head of the country’s Foreign Intelligence Service, and Kyrylo Budanov, who heads the office of the president.
Zelenskyy acknowledged a possible new phase in the negotiations.

“We see on the part of the United States of America, an intensification of talks and meetings,” he told reporters, without mentioning any new proposals. “I myself have spoken with the American side three times in recent days, and I hope for a good result from our negotiators’ meeting.”

Trump had vowed to swiftly end the conflict that began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022. Despite numerous meetings and talks to broker a ceasefire since he took office, the two sides have been locked in a stalemate over the industrial region of Donbas in Ukraine’s east.
